- A brand-new instance now greets you with a welcome screen: name the place, choose the owner's password, point it at a folder of Markdown or a git URL - and land signed in, on your pages. No environment variables, no CLI, nothing to wire by hand.
- One shot, by design: the moment an owner exists, the welcome endpoint is gone. A configured instance cannot be taken over through it, and a failed attempt never leaves you configured-but-broken - the password is stored last, after everything fallible succeeded.
- Env still wins everywhere, so server deployments keep their exact shape. The session secret heals itself too: absent from the env, one is generated once and kept.

## The front door serves you first

- The handbook's home now leads with what every reader actually came for: a five-minute [[Quick start]], then a door for each shape Hanji is lived in - solo, tailnet, agents, publishing. The manifesto still matters; it just stops standing in front of the person mid-task.
- Two guides joined: [[Quick start]] and [[Publish to the web]] - the second one describing exactly how the site you are reading came to exist.
- The published site grew a masthead cover built from the workspace's own landing page, and an optional way home to the site that sent you (`export_home_url`).

## The handbook publishes itself

- `hanji export` grew its browsable half: a static site in the hanji look - warm paper, the serif, the sidebar tree - with not one line of JavaScript. Folders collapse with `<details>`, dark mode rides the system preference, and every link is relative, so the site serves from any path.
- The rendering pipeline moved into its own package, shared verbatim between the web front and the exporter. There is exactly one way Hanji turns Markdown into HTML, and the sanitize rules travel with it.
- Only assets referenced by exported pages ride along: an image on a restricted page stays as dark as the page.
- A `rule` command joined the CLI, so a fresh instance can open content to everyone without touching the front - the piece a publish pipeline needs.
- And this is not hypothetical: the page you are reading is served by that exporter.

## Changes arrive on their own

- Push-to-sync: set one secret, add one webhook to the repository, and a push syncs the matching mount seconds later. Deliveries are signature-verified and answered immediately - the git work happens behind the response, serialized by the same mount lock as every other write. ~~A GitHub App~~ A plain signed webhook: the App, with its registration and installation machinery, was the roadmap's word and would have bought auto-configuration at the price of tying v1 to GitHub. The endpoint speaks to anything that can sign a POST.
- The poll loop: `HANJI_POLL_SECONDS` syncs everything on an interval, because a tailnet has no inbound path for webhooks and polling stays first-class. It also covers local mounts, so edits made outside Hanji show up without asking.

## The export honors the lock, because it is the lock

- `hanji export <dir>` mirrors the workspace as `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, and a per-page `.md` tree - the shape agents on the open web actually read. What lands on disk is exactly what a person with an account and no grants could see: the everyone regime, computed by the same authz predicate as every read in the product. No flag widens an export; mount names only narrow one.
- The exporter refuses a directory it didn't write, refuses an empty everyone-set, and re-exports clean over its own output.

## Agents get the same lock people have

- Token scopes grew a path: `hanji token intern notes/reviews=read` grants one folder, `notes/reviews/draft.md=read+propose` exactly one page. Tokens and people now share a single allow-region mechanism in the one authz predicate; the only asymmetry left is deliberate - "everyone" rules speak to people, never to tokens.
- Old mount-level scopes migrate themselves on the next start; nothing to run.

## The tailnet signs you in

- Tailscale mode: run the instance behind `tailscale serve`, set one variable, and the tailnet's identity signs people in - the owner by env match, everyone else through a login linked on their person sheet. No password typed, no session ceremony. See [[On your tailnet]].
- The mapping answers who, never what: grants stay exactly what the owner assigned, agents stay bearer-token only, and an unlinked tailnet visitor gets a login page that says who it saw and why they are not in yet.
- Trust is opt-in and explicit: the headers are only honored when `HANJI_TAILSCALE_OWNER` is set, and the docs state the deployment contract that makes them unforgeable.

## The lock reaches a single page

- Visibility became content-first, the way every knowledge tool taught people to think: general access (everyone reads, everyone suggests, or restricted) set on a mount, folder, or page, inherited downward, deepest rule wins. People are the exceptions that punch through. Agents never inherit "everyone" - tokens see exactly their scopes.

- Grants grew a path: a person can hold a mount, a folder, or exactly one page. The 1:1 note two people share is invisible to everyone else - tree, search, links, all of it - and a locked page still looks identical to one that does not exist.
- Sharing moved onto the page: a Share button, a name, read or suggest, done. Revoking lands on the person's next request.
- People can now be added bare, with no access at all, and given pages one Share at a time.

## The sidebar becomes a place you organize

- A second pair of hands: the owner adds people in Settings with a name, a password, and per-mount scopes. Viewers read; contributors propose through the same review card as agents. Owner powers stay the owner's.
- Suggest-only mounts opened to people: Update becomes Propose in the editor, and the proposal waits in the same review card an agent's would. One ceremony for every writer.

- A + at the end of every mount, folder, and page row creates a new page in that context. The + on a page nests: the page becomes its section's landing and the new page starts inside it.
- Pages and folders drag: onto a folder or a mount to move there, onto a row's edge to reorder among siblings, onto a page's middle to nest into it. A folder brings its whole subtree, and mounts drag to reorder the rail itself.
- Drops land instantly. The tree moves first, the git work follows, and a failure snaps back with a toast that says why. Reordering is one commit writing `order:` frontmatter; a move is a real `git mv`, so history follows the page.
- Pages can be deleted: a quiet trash next to Edit, armed by a second click, backed by `git rm`. Nothing is truly lost; the repository keeps every sheet.

## Search grew into a real feature

- One backend upgrade: bm25 ranking with a heavy title boost, snippets that mark their hits, prefix matching on the word you are still typing, and multi-word queries ranked by how many of your words a page shares, adjacent phrases first.
- Two surfaces on it: a `⌘K` palette (ranked results, recent pages when empty, keyboard all the way) and a bookmarkable `/kb/search` page with highlighted passages and per-mount filters.
- Agents search through the same ranking, via `hanji_search`.

## The workspace becomes yours

- A workspace name and logo. An SVG adapts its color to light and dark; any other mark gets a mode-safe plate when contrast demands one.
- Colors from three seeds, reinterpreted per mode in OKLCH with readability secured for you, plus curated reading fonts. Your seeds are never altered, only reinterpreted, and the settings page shows which is which.
- Emoji in the editor, three ways: a toolbar picker, `:query` suggestions at the caret, and GitHub-style `:tada:` conversion on the closing colon.
- Proposals left the content list. A card appears under the search box only while something waits, and disappears when the queue is empty.
- Versioning starts at 0.1.0, printed quietly at the bottom of the sidebar.
- A real phone experience: a top bar, a drawer, the same sidebar.

## The agent git flow

- The handbook itself now takes proposals: its mount points at the real repository, so agent contributions to these pages arrive as branches and get reviewed right here.
- Proposals now land in the front: a pending badge in the sidebar, a line diff, and Merge or Reject. Merging is git all the way down: a merge commit on base, the branch deleted, the page and index updated. See [[Proposals]].
- A proposal that no longer merges cleanly opens with a warning and a disabled Merge. No conflict screen, by design: re-propose or reject.
- Along the way the handbook itself found and drove product fixes: sidebar ordering by frontmatter `order`, SVG assets served safely, image width, alignment and captions, local path mounts, a boot smoke test, and an editor that loads only when you edit.

## The editor, and everything around it

- Editable GFM tables, with Notion-style controls: hover handles, boundary insert, drag to move.
- GFM parity in the editor: interactive task-list checkboxes, strikethrough, bare-URL autolinks.
- A collapsible nested sidebar built from page paths, plus a middle-collapsing breadcrumb.
- The editor grew from ~~a block-scoped textarea~~ into a full WYSIWYG surface, with dirty-block byte-fidelity intact.
- A slash menu to insert, image upload into the repo's own `assets/`, and domain-allowlisted embeds.

## v0.1, the foundation

- The byte-fidelity serializer, its corpus gate green on 600-plus real Markdown files.
- The git-backed core: mounts, sync, a SQLite and FTS5 index, permissions on a single read path.
- The MCP agent surface: scoped read tools and propose-as-PR, one bearer token per agent.
- The first web front. Reading only at first, then editing once the craft was locked.

## Decisions we walked back

- Non-Markdown blocks: ~~custom directives~~ plain HTML blocks, so the files stay portable and you can always walk away.
- The editor engine: ~~Tiptap~~ ProseMirror with prosemirror-markdown. We chose byte-fidelity over the faster start.
- The name: ~~kb-rail~~ Hanji. A codename is a placeholder. This one is a promise.

See [[Where we are]] for what is shipping now.

Canvas curves favor the exterior of their project frames, scoring routes by card overlap and time spent inside frames. Direct under-card curves remain a fallback; moved frames update this preference during dragging.

Workspace asks open an integrated conversation above the composer without leaving the current view. ~~The orb opens or minimizes this thread and uses the thinking-orbs library’s tuned 20px breathing/composing variants for presence and activity. Claude/GPT use a light segmented selector.~~ The conductor presence opens the thread, and conductor choice lives in Workspace settings. Selected-card trace controls sit at the top of the canvas, below its toolbar.

---

<!-- handbook/contributing/conventions.md -->

---
title: Conventions
order: 20
description: How the code and the commits are kept.
---

# Conventions

Nothing exotic here. The conventions exist so the codebase stays boring, and boring is the goal.

## Code

- **Strict TypeScript**, everywhere, with no exceptions carved out to dodge a type.
- **Small modules with one job.** The parts of Hanji have clear seams on purpose. A file that grows into two responsibilities gets split.
- **The security-critical paths are single-sourced.** Permissions live in one module. Byte-fidelity lives in one engine. You do not add a second way to do either, because a second way is a second thing to get wrong.
- **No new dependency for what a few lines can do**, and never a dependency that pulls in a model or a meter.

## Commits

- **DCO sign-off** on every commit, `git commit -s`.
- **Clean, human history.** A commit message says what changed and why, in a person's words. No machine trailers, no noise. The point of byte-fidelity is a readable history, and the commits are held to the same bar.
- **One change per commit.** A one-word fix is a one-line diff, and the commit that carries it should be just as legible.

## Documentation

- **Docs ship with the feature.** A behavior change and its handbook pages land in the same series: the changelog says what changed, [[Where we are]] stays true, and the affected guides get swept for claims the change made false. This handbook is the product documenting itself, so a stale page is a product bug.
- **A mechanical floor is enforced by the test suite**: every environment variable the product reads is documented, every CLI command is in the [[Command reference]], every guide page is in the reading order. When that test fails, the docs are wrong, not the test.

## Reviews

Changes get reviewed, and the reviews are adversarial where they need to be, on the permission and byte-fidelity paths especially. A finding on those paths is not a nit. It is the product. Read [[Open core]] for the license this all ships under.

---

<!-- handbook/contributing/develop.md -->

---
title: Developing
order: 10
description: Running the project, and the tests that guard it.
---

# Developing

The project is a pnpm workspace: shared packages, web products and a desktop shell, with TypeScript and Rust. Here is how to run it and how to keep it honest.

## Get set up

- [ ] Obtain an authorized source checkout
- [ ] `pnpm install` (this builds the native SQLite driver, so you need a C toolchain)
- [ ] Set the environment from [[Install Hanji]]
- [ ] `pnpm dev:web` and `pnpm dev:mcp` to run the two surfaces
- [ ] `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm test` before you commit
- [ ] `pnpm test:gates` when you touched the search engine: the suite, then the latency tripwire on its own

## The tests that matter

Run the full suite with `pnpm test`. It covers serialization, authorization, real Git operations, product APIs, canvas behavior and the desktop shell. Two guards are worth calling out.

**The corpus gate.** The serializer's promise is guarded by round-tripping real Markdown files and asserting byte-identity. It is off by default and turns on with `KB_CORPUS_DIR`. It must stay green, and it never gets weakened to make a change pass.

```bash
KB_CORPUS_DIR=/path/to/markdown pnpm vitest run packages/serializer/test/corpus.test.ts
```

**The permission invariant.** Every read flows through one module, and the tests probe it with hostile inputs to make sure a scope can never leak. If you touch reads, you keep them on that one path. Read [[The core]].

**The search bench.** Relevance and latency are measured against judged query
sets that live outside the repo, under `HANJI_BENCH_DIR`: one
`judged-<name>.json` per corpus, each naming the Hanji data dir it is judged
against. The probe prints MRR, hit@1/5/20, the zero-result rate and p50/p95
latency for every set. `HANJI_BENCH_EXCLUDE` holds a term the corpus uses
often (` -foo`, leading space and all), which adds the excluded-term timing
line; without it that line is skipped.

```bash
HANJI_BENCH_DIR=/path/to/bench pnpm exec tsx packages/core/bench/probe.ts
```

## A known gap

The type checker and the unit suite never open the database through the Next app, so a class of runtime binding bug can ship green. A boot smoke test is on the [[Where we are]]. Until it lands, run the front and load a page before you trust a change to the web build.

Read [[Conventions]] for how the code is kept.

<!-- handbook/contributing/index.md -->

---
title: Contributing
order: 40
description: How to get involved, and the state of contributions today.
---

# Contributing

The honest state first. Hanji is pre-release, and it is not accepting external contributions yet. A lightweight contributor agreement will be in place before that opens. So this section is a standing invitation and a map, not an open door quite yet.

## When it opens

Here is what contributing will look like, and what already holds today for anyone building on it.

- Every commit needs a DCO sign-off. Use `git commit -s`. It is the Developer Certificate of Origin, a one-line statement that you wrote the code and can license it.
- The history stays clean and human. Commits read like a person wrote them, because a person did.
- Read [[Developing]] for how to run the project and the tests, [[Conventions]] for how the code is kept, and [[Open core]] for the license and what stays free.

## Bringing your agent

You will likely write your contribution with a coding agent at your side - we do, and this product exists because of that way of working. So the policy is explicit rather than awkward: **agent-assisted contributions are welcome.** A human signs the DCO and answers for the change; the gates - the tests, the corpus round-trip, the leak suite - judge the code without asking who typed it. What we ask is the same thing we ask of any contributor: understand the change you are proposing, keep the history human, and never let an agent negotiate a review for you.

## The spirit

Hanji has a small number of beliefs, listed in [[Principles]], and the code is meant to hold them. A contribution that makes the product faster, clearer, or more honest about its limits is welcome. One that bundles a model, meters a feature, or quietly rewrites the user's files is not, however clever it is. The tie-breakers are the principles, for the code as much as the product.

---

<!-- handbook/contributing/open-core.md -->

---
title: Open core
order: 30
description: The license, the open-core model, and the promise about what stays free.
---

# Open core

Hanji is open core, and the model is chosen deliberately, because the license is a promise you cannot take back later without burning the people who trusted it.

## The license today

The whole project is **AGPL-3.0-only**. That is a strong copyleft license. You can run it, read it, change it, and self-host it freely, and if you offer it as a service, your changes stay open too. It is the terminal license, picked on purpose. There is no plan to relicense, because relicensing is a permanent tax on the trust of everyone who showed up early.

## The seam

Over time, a set of features for administrators will live behind a license key, the way the open-core projects of this era do it. The rule that decides which side of the seam a feature lands on is fixed.

| Free, forever | Paid |
|---|---|
| The complete single-team knowledge base | Single sign-on |
| The editor, history, search | Per-folder granular permissions |
| Bring-your-own-agent, the MCP surface | Audit and enforcement |
| Import and export, the API | Priority support |

The line is simple: never gate what an individual needs to write. A student, a solo maintainer, a small team gets the whole writing experience for nothing, forever. The paid tier is for the things an administrator wants when the team gets big, and only those.

## Where it is today

The paid seam is a plan, not yet code. What ships now is the AGPL core. When the license key and the administrator features arrive, they arrive behind the seam described above, and this page will stop describing a plan and start describing a product. Read [[Mission and vision]] for the why, and the [[Where we are]] for the when.

---

<!-- handbook/guide/activity.md -->

---
title: Workspace insights
order: 47
description: See recorded contributions, trends and the journal across Think, Plan and Document.
---

# Workspace insights

Open **Activity** from the workspace title bar. It belongs to the workspace,
so opening it does not switch you through Document or require Document to be on.
Return to the product you were using when you are ready.

The page opens a usable shell first, then loads the scoped history. A first visit
can take longer while repositories are read. Loading has a visible state, a
bounded wait and a retry action; later visits generally reuse warm data. Refresh
requests current history without replacing the document or losing your filters.

![Workspace insights with fictional contributions](assets/activity-insights.png)

## Read the overview

The overview combines recorded contributions, a seven-day comparison, active
days and the busiest day. Product bars show where activity happened, and the
human/agent split shows the recorded attribution. A chart describes contributions
in the journal, **not hours worked, time saved or a productivity score**. A quiet
chart can mean unrecorded work, not inactivity.

Click a product to narrow the journal. Product, person and human/agent filters
are bookmarkable. Filtering and browser Back update the same page. When a history
read is capped, the interface says so; a partial count is not presented as a
complete history.

## Follow the journal

Entries group by day and describe changes in documents, issues and canvases,
alongside recorded agent work. Runs and sessions can fold related actions into
one readable entry. Follow an entry to the work it describes; choose Older to
continue through history. The overview and the journal serve different scales:
a recent pattern above, the events behind it below.

Each row is scoped to what you can read. A workspace-wide view does not grant
access to another person’s private pages, trackers or canvases. Journal responses
are private and are not a public feed or part of a static documentation export.

![Insights on a narrow screen](assets/activity-insights-mobile.png)

See [[The conductor]] for the agent conversation and [[Permissions]] for the
access model behind the journal.

<!-- handbook/guide/agents.md -->

---
title: Agents
order: 40
description: Connecting a coding agent through the MCP server.
---

# Agents

Agents get their own surface. Two of them, really: raw git, which they already know, and a small MCP server for the times a scoped, hosted read helps. Both go through the same permission check a person does.

## Mint a token

An agent authenticates with a bearer token, scoped to what it may touch - a
whole mount, a folder, or exactly one page on a pages mount (a work mount whole, a think mount whole, a folder of boards or one board), the same path grants people have.

```bash
pnpm hanji token <name> <mount[/folder|/page.md]=read|read+propose|read+comments|...>...
```

```bash
# a read-only agent for the handbook
pnpm hanji token docs-reader handbook=read

# an agent that can also propose changes to two mounts
pnpm hanji token my-claude handbook=read+propose notes=read+propose

# a narrow one: read one folder, propose to a single page
pnpm hanji token intern notes/reviews=read notes/reviews/draft.md=read+propose

# an agent that may also read a page's comments
pnpm hanji token reviewer notes=read+comments
```

The command prints the token once. A `read` scope lets the agent search and read within its grant. A `read+propose` scope adds the right to propose changes there. A `read+comments` scope adds the right to read that page's comments too - stack all three as `read+propose+comments` if the agent needs the full run. There is no `write` scope for a token: editing to base is for people, and an agent always proposes. Anything outside its grants the agent cannot see, and cannot even tell exists - a locked page and a missing page answer identically. Content visibility rules never widen a token: an "everyone" rule speaks to people, and an agent holds exactly what it was granted. See [[Permissions]].

<figure><img src="assets/proposal-review.png" alt="An agent's proposal open for review in the front: title, diff, Reject and Merge"><figcaption>Where a propose lands: a title, a diff, and your decision.</figcaption></figure>

## Connect it

The MCP server speaks Streamable HTTP on `127.0.0.1:4101`. Point your agent at it with the token.

```bash
claude mcp add hanji --transport http http://localhost:4101/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer <token>"
```

## The tools

| Tool | What it does | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| `hanji_list_pages` | List the pages the token can read, 500 at a time, with `nextCursor` for the rest | `read` |
| `hanji_get_page` | Fetch one page's Markdown, or just one section with `anchor` | `read` |
| `hanji_search` | Search across readable mounts: ranked hits, matched and missing terms, a section anchor per hit | `read` |
| `hanji_links` | The link graph around one page: what points here, and where this page points | `read` |
| `hanji_propose` | Propose a page change as a branch, and a PR where GitHub is connected | `read+propose` |
| `hanji_list_comments` | Read one page's comments (threads, quotes, replies) by mount and path | `read+comments` |
| `hanji_changes` | What changed since a moment: commits with authors and pages, edits not yet committed, and comments | `read` |

## What a search answers with

`hanji_search` answers an envelope:

```json
{ "hits": [], "unit": "page", "total": null, "totalAny": null, "facets": null,
  "missingEverywhere": [], "suggestions": [], "undated": 0, "nextOffset": null,
  "state": "indexing" }
```

Each hit carries `mount`, `path`, `title`, `snippet`, `score`, `matched`, `missing`, `marks`, `headingPath`, `anchor`, `passages` and `updatedAt`. Read them in that order of trust. `snippet` is the short preview - `passages[0]` when a passage actually got cut, falling back to the page's own description and then its title on a full-search hit whose cut comes back blank. A `tier: "title"` hit is the exception: it carries only `title`, `mount`, `path` and `score`, with `snippet`, `headingPath`, `anchor`, `passages`, `matched`, `missing` and `marks` empty and `updatedAt` null. `matched` and `missing` say which of your terms the page actually holds, after aliases and stemming, so a hit that is missing the term you care about is one you can drop without reading it; `marks` names the spellings actually found in the text, which is how a page reached through a synonym tells you which word it really uses. `score` ranks within one response and is normalized per query: it is not comparable across queries, and thresholding on it is a mistake. There is no `coverage` field to filter on. `missingEverywhere` names the terms that matched nothing anywhere in the scope you asked for, your grants and any `mount` or `pathPrefix` filter included.

An envelope carrying `state: "indexing"` means the index is currently being rebuilt: the empty `hits` reflect that window, so retry once the rebuild finishes rather than reading it as an empty corpus. The field is absent the rest of the time.

`anchor` is the hit's best section, written `<block_hash>:<ord>` - empty on a title-tier hit, since a title match has no section behind it. Hand a non-empty anchor straight to `hanji_get_page` and you get that section's Markdown instead of the whole page. If the block has been edited since, the answer is the whole page with `anchorResolved: false`, never "Not found." - that string keeps its one meaning, which is "you may not see this, or it does not exist".

| Parameter | Values | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `limit` | 1-50, default 20 | Hits to return |
| `offset` | 0-499 | Skips ahead through the 500 best matches; `nextOffset` comes back `null` once you have them all |
| `mount` | a mount name | Narrows to one mount - curl's `mount=`, a separate parameter from the web search palette's `m=` |
| `pathPrefix` | a folder name, or a prefix | No slash matches that folder name at any depth; a slash makes it a literal prefix |
| `granularity` | `page` \| `section` | `section` returns one hit per section instead of one per page; the envelope's `unit` reports back which |
| `tier` | `title` | A name lookup instead of a search: title-only, at most 8 rows, no passages, ignoring `mount`, `pathPrefix` and `since` |
| `exact` | boolean | Computes `total`, `totalAny` and `facets` too - a second, unbounded pass most callers skip |
| `suggest` | boolean | Fills `suggestions` with page matches when nothing hit; otherwise the array stays empty |
| `bigramPrefix` | boolean | Lets a single Korean syllable match as a prefix, for a query still being typed |
| `since` | ISO 8601 timestamp | Drops pages with no date and counts them in `undated`; compares on the calendar day, since a page's own date can be date-only, while `hanji_changes` compares on the instant; an invalid value is a 400 naming the expected format over curl, and a tool error over MCP |

## Paging the page list

`hanji_list_pages` answers `{ pages, nextCursor }`, 500 rows at a time. Narrow it first with `mount` or `pathPrefix`, the same two filters search takes, or raise `limit` up to 2000 if 500 rows at a time is too chatty.

Pass `nextCursor` back as `cursor` until it comes back null. A cursor is a position, never a permission: decoding it only tells the query where to resume, and that resume point still runs inside your own scope. A cursor minted for a mount you cannot read decodes fine and simply skips you forward through whatever you may see - it reaches nothing wider. Only a cursor that decodes to nothing readable as a position gets refused - garbled, or not one of ours - a 400 over curl, a tool error over MCP.

## What links answers with

`hanji_links` returns `{ backlinks, outlinks }`.

A backlink carries `mount`, `path`, `title` and `via: "title" | "stem"` - which kind of name the linking page used to reach this one. It also carries `ambiguous: true` when that name, title or path stem, belongs to more than one page you can read, so you know a plain link by that name could have landed on any of them. A page linking here by both its title and its stem still appears once in `backlinks`, credited to `via: "title"`.

An outlink carries `text` plus `mount`, `path` and `title` when it resolves to a page you can read. When it does not, it carries `text` alone - the same shape a dangling link gets, so a link to a page outside your grant reads identically to a link to nothing at all.

## No MCP client? curl works

Every tool is also a plain HTTP endpoint on the same port, same token, no
JSON-RPC envelope and no streaming to parse. For scripts, cron jobs, and
agents that can run a shell but not an MCP client:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "http://localhost:4101/pages?limit=100"
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "http://localhost:4101/page?mount=handbook&path=install.md"
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "http://localhost:4101/page?mount=handbook&path=install.md&anchor=1k2j3h4:0"
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "http://localhost:4101/search?q=permissions&limit=5" | jq '.hits[].path'
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "http://localhost:4101/links?mount=handbook&path=install.md"
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "http://localhost:4101/comments?mount=notes&path=idea.md"
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "http://localhost:4101/changes?since=2026-08-27T00:00:00Z" | jq '.items[].subject'
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "http://localhost:4101/propose" \
  -d '{"mount":"notes","path":"ideas/from-cron.md","title":"An idea","content":"# It\n","note":"Confident on wording; check the anchor link."}'
```

`/pages`, `/search`, `/links`, `/comments` and `/changes` answer JSON; `/page`
answers raw Markdown, or JSON `{ content, anchorResolved }` when you pass an
anchor - an empty `anchor=` still counts as passing one, and gets that same
JSON form back with `anchorResolved: false`, the shape a stale anchor answers
with too. `/propose` answers the branch (and PR URL where GitHub is
connected). The permission check is the same one the MCP tools run, and an
unknown path answers with a map of the surface.

`/search`, `/pages`, `/page`, `/links`, `/changes` and `/comments` are strict
about their query string: a parameter they do not recognize, misspelled or
otherwise, is a 400 naming it, never a filter silently dropped. Every MCP tool
refuses the same way, naming the key in a tool error. A blank value (`&since=`)
counts as no value at all, the same as leaving the parameter off entirely. A
boolean parameter takes `true`, `false`, `1` or `0` and nothing else.

**Four things changed shape in 0.7.** `/search` answered a bare array and
now answers the envelope above. `/pages` answered every row and now answers
`{ pages, nextCursor }`, 500 at a time. `/changes` answered a bare array and
now answers `{ items, truncated }`, with each item's `paths` capped at twenty
and the rest counted in `omittedPaths`. And all three got strict, along with
`/page`, `/links` and `/comments`: a stray parameter used to be silently
ignored, and a `limit` over the bound used to be silently clamped - both are
a 400 over curl now, and a tool error over MCP, on every tool. If you have
a script reading the old shapes, `.hits`, `.pages` and `.items` are the one
edit each needs.

## Propose, do not overwrite

`hanji_propose` is the only write an agent has, and it never touches base directly - see below for the shape of it, and [[Proposals]] for where it lands.

## Start the session with what changed

`hanji_changes` (and `GET /changes?since=…`) answers the question a returning agent should ask first: what moved since I last read? Commits with their authors and pages, a local mount's edits not yet committed (one row per mount, timed by the newest file), and new comments, across exactly the mounts the token can read. Items authored by Hanji itself (the digest's own commits) carry the actor class `hanji` - housekeeping labeled as itself, so an agent can skip it when briefing. The intended habit: ask at session start, then brief your human in two lines instead of making them scroll. Reads freshen local mounts first (throttled to about once per ten seconds), so the answer is at most a few seconds behind the files - and there is an Atom projection of the same feed at `/feed.atom?token=<token>` for feed readers and bots (no token serves only what is open to everyone, the same rule a published site follows).

The answer is `{ items, truncated }`, never a bare array. `limit` takes 1 to 500 items, default 100. Each item's `paths` is capped at twenty, with anything past that counted in `omittedPaths` - the twenty an agent sees are sliced from the already-filtered list, so they are always twenty it may see. `truncated: true` means a 256 kB response budget stopped the list short of `limit`, a byte cap that has nothing to do with what the token can read.

## Propose, and say what you are unsure about

A proposal accepts an optional `note`: the agent's own self-review, riding the commit body under the title. Say what you are confident about and what you are not - it shows on the review card and makes the human's yes faster. An honest "unsure whether the old anchor still resolves" is worth more than a confident silence.

`hanji_propose` never edits a page in place. It creates a branch named for the change and commits the new content there. On a clone mount it pushes the branch to the mount's remote, and if `HANJI_GITHUB_TOKEN` is set, it also opens a pull request and hands back the URL. On a local mount the branch stays in the folder's own repository: nothing is pushed and no pull request is opened. A proposal on a local mount is refused while the page differs in the folder from its base branch (an edit the owner has not committed yet). When the repository refuses the change (a git hook, commit signing), the answer is `Proposal failed: the repository refused the change.`, and the reason goes to the server's log. A person reviews it and merges. That is the whole point. An agent can suggest all day, and nothing lands in your knowledge base until someone says yes.

Where does the suggestion go? Straight into the front: see [[Proposals]] for the review-and-merge side of this loop.

## Agents inside Hanji Plan

An agent that Hanji Plan runs (a session, a thread ask, the conductor) holds one Document identity: a token named `agent-<handle>`, minted once by the owner: `pnpm hanji token agent-scribe docs=read+propose`.

Hanji's own reads for that agent go through that token. `tracker kb` and `tracker lint` under `TRACKER_AS=agent:<handle>` list and check only the pages the token reads; a thread's prompt and the conductor's brief name only those pages; and a Claude session gets `hanji_search`, `hanji_get_page` and `hanji_propose` as tools the host serves in process, with no MCP server running and no secret in the session. `hanji_propose` answers the proposal's link in Document's review, where a person merges it. With no token, Hanji's tools, prompts and briefs give the agent no page and no way to propose. Pages stay at `read+propose`: the agent proposes, a person merges. `pnpm hanji revoke-token agent-scribe` ends the identity; a session already running keeps its tools until it sleeps, and its next start finds none.

The conductor, the standing session about the whole workspace, is one conversation per person. It holds the agent's token for pages and acts within the rights of the person it talks to, read at each call, so a grant removed mid-conversation applies at the next. Teammates get a conversation of their own once the owner turns teammates on: `conductor: {teammates: true}` in the tracker file, counted only when Workspace settings in Hanji Plan saved it, so an edit by hand or by a session opens nothing; theirs runs with none of the owner's settings and only the workspace's tools.

In Hanji Document, Hanji Plan and Hanji Think the conductor's panel is the same conversation; its tools edit pages for you (`hanji_edit`), change boards (`think_apply`) and open places (`open`) within your rights and the token's grants. Every page, board and issue a tool returns is marked as text its author wrote, so a sentence planted in a page is data to the conductor.

A session's log is readable by everyone who can view the tracker, whatever their grants on the docs mount: its first message, the pages its tools returned and its replies included. Grant the agent's token only pages that audience may read.

The token scopes Hanji's tools, prompts and briefs only. The tracker CLI names the agent through `TRACKER_AS`, which a session can unset, or set to `owner` or `user:<name>`, to read as the owner; and the session's environment holds the data folder, so it can run `hanji` itself. A session also runs Claude Code with the person's own settings, so a tool call those settings allow can read or edit any file the operating-system user can, a local docs mount included. The operating-system user is the boundary.

Read [[Command reference]] for the rest of the CLI.

---

<!-- handbook/guide/cli.md -->

---
title: Command reference
order: 50
description: Every Hanji CLI command, in one table.
---

# Command reference

The whole CLI, run as `pnpm hanji <command>`. It reads `HANJI_DATA_DIR` for where to work, defaulting to `~/.hanji`.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `add-mount <name> <repoUrl> <mountPath> [subpath] [--suggest] [--local] [--kind pages\|work\|think]` | Add a repository, or a folder of one, as a mount, and print its kind. `--suggest` makes it proposal-only; `--local` mounts a folder on this machine in place, stored as its absolute path; `--kind` sets the kind by hand (see [[Mounts]]). |
| `remove-mount <name>` | Remove a mount and its indexed pages. The clone directory stays on disk. |
| `sync` | Fetch every pages mount from its remote and reindex what changed. Plan and think mounts are left to Plan and Think. |
| `rebuild` | Discard the index and rebuild it from the local clones. Always safe. |
| `token <name> <mount[/folder\|/page.md]=read\|read+propose\|read+comments\|read+propose+comments>...` | Mint a bearer token for an agent, scoped to a mount, or on a pages mount a folder or one page - add `+comments` to also grant that scope's page comments. Prints it once. |
| `revoke-token <name>` | End a token by its name. Its grants go with it: an MCP client that held it is refused from its next request; a Hanji Plan session keeps its Document tools until it sleeps, and its next start finds none. |
| `list` | List every mount with its kind, and how many pages each pages mount holds. |
| `export <outDir> [mount...] [--okf]` | Publish everything open to everyone: a browsable static site, `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, and every page as plain Markdown. Mount names narrow the set; nothing widens it. `--okf` also shapes the Markdown mirror into an [Open Knowledge Format](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/open-knowledge-format) bundle, described in [[Publish to the web]]. |
| `rule <mount> [path] <everyone-read\|everyone-propose\|restricted\|clear>` | Set or clear a general-access rule from the command line - what Share's select does in the front. |
| `set <key> <value>` | Write an instance setting from the table below. |
| `tools [write,work,think]` | Print the tools this workspace has on, or set them: a comma-joined list of `write`, `work` and `think`, at least one. Turning a tool off keeps its mount and its files; a mount added for a tool that is off waits until the tool is on. |
| `assets [mount]` | List uploaded images no page references anymore, per mount or everywhere. |
| `digest <mount> [path] [--since <iso>]` | Document "what changed, what awaits you" as a Markdown page into the mount (default `digest.md`), committed by Hanji itself. Covers since the previous digest; a quiet window with an empty review queue writes nothing. |

One caution on `digest`: the page is written with the owner's eyes and summarizes the whole workspace, so it belongs in a mount whose readers may see all of that. In a mixed-audience workspace, point it at a restricted mount.

## Examples

```bash
pnpm hanji add-mount handbook git@github.com:you/product.git handbook docs
pnpm hanji sync
pnpm hanji token my-claude handbook=read+propose
pnpm hanji list

# the digest as a morning ritual: cron writes the page, you and your
# agents read it like any other page - no mail server involved
# 0 7 * * *  cd /path/to/hanji && pnpm hanji digest notes
pnpm hanji digest notes
```

## The settings it holds

`hanji set <key> <value>` writes these, and Settings in the front writes the same rows except the last. They live in `config.db`, the durable database; the index can be rebuilt at any time and never holds them.

| Key | What it sets |
|---|---|
| `workspace_name` | The name in the sidebar and on the published site. |
| `workspace_mode` | Whether this instance runs as one person's or a team's. |
| `search_aliases` | `<mount name>/<page path>` of the page declaring this knowledge base's synonym classes, written `term = alias, alias` or as a two-column table row - see [[Reading and writing]]. Unset means no aliases. |
| `search_log` | `off` turns off the local query log; default on. The log lives in `config.db`, so an entry outlives the page it names, and no principal is recorded with it: on a shared workspace every reader's queries land in the same table. |
| `theme_accent` | The workspace's one accent, as `#rrggbb` (near black when unset); light and dark follow the system. |
| `conductor_visual` | Workspace conductor shape and per-state motions, stored as validated JSON by Settings, Appearance. |
| `theme_font` | The reading font for prose in Document: `newsreader`, `literata`, `source-serif` or `inter`. |
| `appearance_v2` | Set once by the first open after the one-accent change, which cleared the earlier default accents; the retired keys `theme_background`, `theme_text`, `theme_mode`, `theme_dark_accent`, `theme_dark_background`, `theme_dark_text`, `theme_dark_auto` stay in the table unread. |
| `content_width`, `content_size` | The reading column's width and type size. |
| `logo`, `logo_adapt`, `logo_hidden`, `logo_luma`, `logo_coverage` | The workspace logo and how it adapts to the theme behind it. |
| `sidebar_collapse` | Whether the sidebar starts collapsed. |
| `tools` | The tools this workspace has on, `write,work,think` in that order; written once from the mounts when a workspace is first opened by this version, then by `tools` and by Settings. |
| `export_site_label`, `export_home_label`, `export_home_url`, `export_edit_base_url` | What a published site calls itself, where its home link goes, and where "suggest an edit" lands. See [[Publish to the web]]. |
| `session_secret`, `owner_password_hash` | Written by Hanji on first run and read on every login. Not for hand-editing; `HANJI_SESSION_SECRET` and `HANJI_OWNER_PASSWORD` override them. |

## The environment it reads

| Variable | Used by | For |
|---|---|---|
| `HANJI_DATA_DIR` | everything, `tracker-host` included | Where clones and the index live. Defaults to `~/.hanji`. |
| `HANJI_SESSION_SECRET` | the front | Signs login sessions. Optional - first run generates and stores one; env overrides. |
| `HANJI_OWNER_PASSWORD` | the front | The owner's password. Optional - the welcome screen stores one on first run; env overrides. |
| `HANJI_GITHUB_TOKEN` | propose | Lets `hanji_propose` open real pull requests on a clone mount; a local mount's proposal opens none. |
| `HANJI_GIT_AUTHOR_NAME`, `HANJI_GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL` | writes | The name and email on the owner's commits. The name wins over the one set in Settings → People (Settings → General while the workspace has no people); with neither, commits read Hanji Owner. |
| `PORT` | the MCP server | The port it listens on. Defaults to 4101. |
| `HANJI_TAILSCALE_OWNER` | the front, Hanji Plan, Hanji Think | Turns on [[On your tailnet]] and names the owner's tailnet login. The login signs a request in only when its `Host` is the loopback address or the host of one of the three product addresses below. |
| `HANJI_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | the front | Turns on push-to-sync at `/api/webhook/git`; deliveries must carry its signature. |
| `HANJI_POLL_SECONDS` | the front | Sync every pages mount on this interval. The mechanism for tailnets and local mounts. |
| `HANJI_TRACKER_URL` | the front, Hanji Plan, Hanji Think | Plan's address, where `[[HNJ-12]]`, Cited by and a board's **Open** links open an issue. Defaults to `http://127.0.0.1:4102`. On a tailnet, set it to Plan's `tailscale serve` address; its host is then a `Host` that the tailnet login signs in. |
| `HANJI_KB_URL` | the front, Hanji Plan (its web app and its session host), Hanji Think | Where links to Document pages point. Defaults to `http://127.0.0.1:4100`. On a tailnet, its host is a `Host` that the tailnet login signs in. See [[On your tailnet]]. |
| `HANJI_THINK_URL` | the front, Hanji Plan, Hanji Think | Where links to Hanji Think boards point: `[[board:boards/crit#9f2c]]` in a page, and an issue's **From** link in Plan. Defaults to `http://127.0.0.1:4104`. On a tailnet, its host is a `Host` that the tailnet login signs in. Think on a tailnet needs the `tailscale serve` host named by this address or by one of the other two. |
| `HANJI_VERSION` | the front | Set by the build from the repository's package.json: the version in the workspace menu. |

For the agent side of this, read [[Agents]]. For what is coming, read [[Where we are]].

## Whiteboard development commands

The [[Think canvas]] has its own launcher, `node --import tsx packages/whiteboard/src/main.ts`, which reads `HANJI_DATA_DIR` like the rest. With no subcommand it serves every board of the workspace's think mounts on `--port` (4104) and, in a terminal, prints the owner's access link; `--demo` serves a throwaway workspace with one seeded board; `--repo` and `--state` are refused, except that `migrate-board` takes `--state`. `key --agent <handle>` prints an agent key, `key --revoke <handle>` ends one, `key --rotate-owner` replaces the owner's, and `key --owner-link` prints the owner's link again. `read`, `ops --file <request.json>` and `mcp` take `--board <mountPath>/<folder>` and require `WHITEBOARD_TOKEN`; MCP uses stdio. `migrate-board --board <mountPath>/<folder> --state <old state folder>` moves a board from the first launcher into a folder of its mount, with its journal. `WHITEBOARD_URL` is used only by the figure scripts and `scripts/whiteboard-browser.mjs`, and should be an access link to a fictional demo board. `pnpm tracker-host` runs the session host over `HANJI_DATA_DIR` alone: it opens every registered tracker, and `TRACKER_WORKSPACE` adds a folder that is not registered, which then leads, while Plan is on (with Plan off the host opens no tracker, says so at start, and an issue's or a project's session waits until Plan is on), and a workspace of pages or boards alone has a conductor too. A second host on the same data folder exits with code 3. The `tracker` CLI acts on `TRACKER_WORKSPACE`, else on the workspace above the current directory; `tracker --tracker <PREFIX> <verb>` names a registered tracker by its prefix (exact case; it wins over both), and a prefix no mount holds fails with the registered ones listed.

---

<!-- handbook/guide/comments.md -->

---
title: Comments
order: 35
description: A place to talk about a page, right on the page.
---

# Comments

Every page ends in a quiet thread. Anyone who can read the page can read what is said there, and add to it too - comments are discussion, not page content, so reading is the only right that gates them.

## What a comment is

A comment sits at the bottom of the page, under its own heading, separate from the prose above it. Write a note - **⌘B** and **⌘I** format as you go, a line starting with `-` or `1.` becomes a list, and `:` opens the same emoji menu the page editor uses - then press **Comment**, or just press Enter (Shift+Enter starts a new line). It appears with your name and when you wrote it. Reply to any comment once - replies are one level deep, so a thread stays a conversation, not a maze. The comment's author, or the workspace owner, can edit it afterward (an edited comment carries a quiet "edited" mark), resolve a thread (it fades but stays readable), or delete a comment outright; everyone else reads.

This is Hanji's version of the sticky note on a shared page: for the aside that is not worth its own edit, the question for a reader before you make a change, the "looks good" that closes a loop. It is not a change to the page and never a substitute for one.

## What a comment is not

Comments never enter git. They live in Hanji's own metadata store, next to mounts, users, and permissions, and they never become a commit, a file, or a line anyone `git blame`s. Export a mount to the static site or `llms.txt`, and comments do not ride along - the export, and the open web it feeds, carry the page alone. (An agent on the live MCP can read them, but only with an explicit grant - see below.)

That also means a comment follows the page's own life in git: move a page and its comments move with it, delete a page and its comments go too. Nothing is ever left pointing at a path that no longer exists.

## Commenting on a word or a sentence

A comment does not have to be about the whole page. Select a run of prose - a word, a sentence, a paragraph - and a small bar appears over it offering **Copy** and **Comment**, and **Issue** when you can file work into one of the workspace's trackers (see below). Press **Comment** and the composer opens right there, already focused, ready to type. (The bar is deliberate: a selection used to open the composer outright, which took the selection with it, so you could not simply copy the words you had just picked out. Now commenting is one press further on, and the text stays yours until you ask for it.) Post the note, and the selection carries a mark from then on: every reader sees the same quiet wash of the workspace accent over that exact phrase.

An annotation's wash is not the same thing as a [[Reading and writing|highlight]] you apply yourself. The wash is Hanji showing you where a note is anchored, in one fixed color of its own apart from the workspace accent, and it lives in Hanji's own store; a highlight is content, it is one of four colours you chose, and it is written into the file.

A comment needs a single block to anchor to, so a selection spanning two paragraphs offers **Copy** alone.

These anchored notes live in a panel beside the page, not in the thread at its foot. Open it from the comment icon in the page header, or just click a highlighted phrase and the panel opens with that note scrolled to and lit. It lists every annotation on the page, filters by open or resolved, and lets you reply or resolve without leaving your place in the text. Each thread leads with the quote it was written against, wearing the same highlight the phrase wears in the prose, so the note reads clearly even with the page scrolled away.

That link is best-effort, not permanent. Edit the block the quote lives in, and if the quote no longer matches what is there, the note detaches: it moves down into "On an earlier version" at the foot of the panel, still showing the exact words it was written against, but no longer painted into the prose. The note is not lost, only its anchor is - the words it once pointed at have moved on.

Inline highlights use the browser's CSS Custom Highlight API, which needs a fairly current engine (recent Chrome, Edge, or Safari). On an older browser without it, the panel and its quoted text still read fine - only the painted highlight in the prose is missing.

## Filing an issue from a sentence

A doc review often turns a sentence into a task. When the workspace has a tracker that you can edit (or several), and your Hanji name is one of that tracker file's `people:` or you are the owner, the selection bar also offers **Issue**. It opens a small form beside the text: the title starts as the words you selected, and you can edit it. Hanji keeps the title on one line and cuts a longer one at 120 characters. The project is filled in when the page links exactly one project with `[[project:HNJ/<slug>]]`. With several trackers you can edit, the form asks which one, and the project is filled in from the page's link to that tracker's project. Press **Create issue**.

The issue is one commit in the tracker, made as you. Its body quotes your selection, and its `source:` names this page by its file stem and the heading above the selection, for example `source: review#Budget`. A selection above the first heading names the page alone. Hanji writes nothing to the page. Its Cited by line shows the new issue immediately, and the notice links to it in Plan.

Press **Issue** twice, or file the same words under the same heading again, and you get the issue already filed: the notice says "Filed as HNJ-12". A new issue's notice offers **Undo** for ten seconds, its button or `⌘Z` / `Ctrl+Z` while it shows and your cursor is outside a text field, and it waits while you point at the notice or move focus into it. Undo cancels that issue in one commit, and its key is never given to another issue. A new issue's notice takes focus as it appears, unless you have already moved into another field, so from the keyboard Tab reaches **Open** and then **Undo**. Escape closes the notice. When it closes with focus inside it, by Undo, by Escape or when the ten seconds end, and after a "Filed as" notice, focus is on the paragraph you selected from. A canceled issue does not count, so the same sentence can be filed again. Undo never touches an issue someone filed before you.

Like a comment, an issue needs a selection inside one block.

## Agents and comments

Comments are a human side-channel by default. An agent reads them only through an explicit `read+comments` scope on its token (or `read+propose+comments`), and only on pages it can already read - a token without the capability sees nothing, the same as a page that does not exist. See [[Agents]] for the token grammar and `hanji_list_comments`.

## What's here now

Both forms of comment ship: a thread at the foot of the page for the page as a whole, and anchored threads for a specific word or sentence - highlighted right where they were written, and gathered in a panel beside the prose, reached from the page header or by clicking any highlight.

---

<!-- handbook/guide/conductor.md -->

---
title: The conductor
order: 46
description: One conversation per person, in a panel at the corner of Hanji Document, Hanji Plan and Hanji Think.
---

# The conductor

The conductor is the workspace's standing conversation with its agent. Each person has one, and it is the same conversation in Hanji Document, Hanji Plan and Hanji Think: a panel at the bottom right corner of every page, canvas and issue, a pill until you press it or ⌘J (Ctrl+J off macOS). The conversation runs on the owner's computer, through the session host (`pnpm tracker-host` from a checkout, with the workspace's `HANJI_DATA_DIR`).

![The conductor panel in Hanji Document, after an edit, with Undo on the row](assets/conductor-write.png)

In Think, the canvas also shows tool activity: a reading/editing/approval badge and a labeled cursor using your selected conductor shape, primary color and state motion, at explicit tool targets, and brief object highlights after an update. It follows your conductor’s actual tool events, keeps off-screen work in a badge, and never pans the canvas just to show activity. See [[Think canvas]].

## What it knows

Every message carries where you are. A page in Document adds `Looking at page:docs/guide.md: Guide`, the selection when you have one, and whether the page has unsaved changes; an issue or a view in Plan adds the issue or the view; a canvas in Think adds the board, the selected objects and the visible area. In Think, **Ask conductor** on an object or selection prepares a request to improve its structure and connections. It appends to an existing draft and opens the composer without sending. The chip above the composer shows the line that will go with your message; its × drops it for that message. A page the agent reads comes back to it marked as text its author wrote, so a sentence planted in a page is data to the conductor.

## What it can do

Within your rights and the agent's token, the conductor reads pages, boards and issues, edits a page for you (`hanji_edit`, as the agent with you as co-author, so the page's byline reads "Updated by scribe for Ada · Undo"), changes a board (`think_apply`, with the same authorship on the board's history; its `content` parameter inserts Brainstorm, Retrospective and Decision flow templates or up to 50 sticky notes from a list), opens a place in any of the three products (`open`), and proposes where it may not edit. An edit to a page you are not looking at, a change that deletes more than ten objects, or a change to a board you are neither looking at nor naming asks you first: Allow or Deny, in the panel.

![The conductor panel in Hanji Plan on an issue, with the conversation and a Back chip](assets/conductor-work.png)

## Moving across the products

When the conductor opens a place, the tab you asked from follows it, and the conversation continues there with a Back chip. Another tab with the same conversation open shows a chip and stays where it is. A key pressed since Send keeps you where you are, too.

![The conductor panel in Hanji Think after a change to the board, with Show and Undo on its row](assets/conductor-think.png)

## Undo

Every change the conductor made is a row with Undo beside it: a page goes back to its previous revision as you, a board's change is reversed as you, and the next checkpoint credits the undo to you. Document's byline carries the same Undo while the page's last edit was the conductor's for you. A change to a board that added comments or reactions, or deleted objects that had them, cannot be reversed, and the panel says so; so does a board that moved on since.

## Teammates

By default the conductor answers the owner alone. The teammates switch on Hanji Plan's Agents page gives each teammate a conversation of their own, which the owner can read ("Ada can read this conversation. It runs on Ada's computer.", said once). A teammate's conversation runs with the agent's own settings alone, none of the owner's, and reaches only what that teammate may read.

## When the panel says something else

- "Session host is not running": start it from a checkout with the workspace's `HANJI_DATA_DIR`; the Agents page in Hanji Plan shows the command.
- "Claude Code is not installed": the host found no `claude` on its PATH; install Claude Code, or start the session host with `CLAUDE_BIN` naming the claude binary.
- "scribe reads no page yet" (the agent's handle first): the agent has no token; the owner's panel in Hanji Document offers one checkbox per mount and a button that mints `read+propose` on each (`pnpm hanji token agent-<handle> <mount>=read+propose` does the same).
- "The conductor is not available; ask Ada": the workspace's conductor is a Codex agent, which answers the owner alone.

## Appearance settings

In **Settings → Appearance → Conductor**, choose Orb, Ring, Crystal, Blob, Cube or Disc. The indicator uses the workspace primary color. Each state—Paused, Open, Active and Working—has a motion choice: Still, Gentle sway, Rotate or Breathe. These change the indicator's appearance, not the agent's capabilities or permissions. Reduced motion keeps it still.

---

<!-- handbook/guide/desktop.md -->

---
title: Desktop workspace
order: 11
description: Install the invited Mac preview, create a workspace, and move between Think, Plan and Document.
---

# Desktop workspace

Hanji brings **Think**, **Plan** and **Document** into one Mac workspace. The
current desktop preview is shared by invitation; public binary downloads are
not available yet. [Request access and read the setup guide](https://hanji.ink/start/).
The app includes its runtime, so a preview recipient does not need to install
Node, pnpm or a coding agent to use the basic tools.

## Install and open

Unzip the preview you received and read **Start here.html**. Move **Hanji.app**
to **Applications**, then open it there. Use the build shared for your Mac.
Signing and notarization depend on that build. If macOS cannot verify it, confirm
its source with the person sharing it and follow
[Apple’s guidance](https://support.apple.com/102445).

![First launch](assets/onboarding-desktop-home.png)

Choose **Create your workspace**. Existing workspaces can be opened from their
data folder, and a team workspace can be opened using its supplied address.
A team address requires the network and access its owner has configured;
entering an address does not grant permissions.

## Four short setup stages

1. **Your workspace.** Give it a name and choose products. Think, Plan and
   Document begin selected. You can change the selection in Settings later.
2. **Your content.** Start fresh lets Hanji prepare local folders for the selected
   products, including an editable welcome page in Document. Bring existing
   content asks only for the sources those products need.
3. **Secure access.** Choose and confirm an owner password of at least eight
   characters. Keep it safe. This Mac signs you in automatically; the password
   protects owner access outside the desktop app.
4. **Review and begin.** Check the workspace, content and access before creating.
   Edit links return to the relevant stage with in-memory choices preserved.

![Review the workspace before creating it](assets/onboarding-review.png)

The name, product choices and fresh/import choice survive a reload in that tab.
Passwords are never saved in the draft. Quick setup help opens inside the flow.
A failed setup can be corrected or retried; newly created folders and mounts
roll back before the owner account is stored. Existing files are preserved.

## Move between products

The title bar switches between Think, Plan and Document. Activity and Settings
are independent workspace views. The workspace menu opens another workspace or
returns to the workspace list. A workspace may use one, two or all three products.

Shared search controls, sidebars, the primary color, appearance and the conductor
follow the workspace. The products keep their own content and editing tools:

- [[Think canvas]] explores ideas with spatial objects and shared workshops.
- [[Objectives and key results]] connects goals to the issues in Plan.
- [[Reading and writing]] keeps knowledge in Markdown through Document.
- [[Workspace insights]] follows recorded work across all three.

## Add an agent when you need one

The conductor uses your configured Claude or Codex setup. It does not include a
model subscription, and ordinary reading, editing and canvas work do not require
one. Agent access follows the workspace’s permissions and token scopes; requested
approvals remain explicit. [[The conductor]] explains context, approval and Undo.

The implementation still uses identifiers such as `write`, `work`, `tracker`
and `whiteboard` in package names, commands, storage and URLs. Those are technical
identifiers for Document, Plan and Think; the product names above describe the UI.

For an existing source checkout or a server, use [[Install Hanji]].

---

<!-- handbook/guide/idea-to-action.md -->

---
title: From idea to action
order: 25
description: Follow one decision through Think, Plan and Document without losing its reasoning.
---

# From idea to action

Hanji explores clearer interaction between people and agents. Its current workspace brings exploration, execution and knowledge into one place. This guide follows a small fictional project, **First mile**, to show how the three surfaces can make context and decisions easier to understand. It is a worked example, not a customer result or a promise that every handoff happens automatically.

The question: **How could a new teammate experience value before configuring a workspace?**

## 1. Explore the question in Think

Create a canvas and write the question first. Add the alternatives, their trade-offs and what you need to learn. For First mile, Ada and Noor compare a guided setup with an editable starter project.

![First mile canvas: the question, two alternatives, the decision and the next step](assets/public-canvas.png)

Keep the decision visible beside the alternatives: **try a working example first**. That preserves the reasoning when someone returns to the canvas later. Use notes and connectors directly; an agent is optional. [[Think canvas]] explains creation, editing and workshops.

## 2. Give the next step an owner in Plan

Select the next-step note and use **Create issue**. Choose the destination and review what will be created. In Plan, give the issue an owner and a clear completion condition. See [[Links and references]] for supported links and references.

For this example, the issue is **Create the editable starter project**. It is ready when the project opens with a clear first task, its content can be changed and removed, and imported work stays separate. A follow-up issue tests the first session in a fresh workspace.

![The starter-project issue with its decision, completion criteria and review](assets/public-plan-issue.png)

A task tells someone what to do. Its connection to the original question helps them decide how to do it. Add explicit references to the canvas and the decision page where useful; moving between surfaces does not turn every relationship into a dependency automatically.

## 3. Keep the decision in Document

Write a short record: the question, the alternatives, the decision, its trade-offs and the next review. Think's **Write up** action can start a page from selected objects; review the result in Document and add the context you want to keep.

![A decision record describing the two directions and what the team still needs to learn](assets/document-reading.png)

The record should distinguish what the team chose from what it has validated. In this example, the editable project is a direction to test. It is not evidence that onboarding has improved. Record observations after the test, including reasons to change course.

## Bring an agent in when useful

Open the conductor from the canvas, issue or page. Check the context chip before sending. You might ask it to compare the selected alternatives, clarify completion criteria or propose a decision summary. Review the response and any requested changes. [[The conductor]] explains context, approvals and Undo; [[Permissions]] explains the different access boundaries.

## What the interface should make clear

Before asking an agent to help, check what context you are sharing. After its response, distinguish the suggestion from the decision you have actually made. When it changes something, inspect the affected content and use the available history, approval or Undo controls where supported.

In this example, an agent could help compare the onboarding alternatives or draft the decision record. The people still need to judge the trade-offs and test the result. A clear account of the question, the contribution and the decision helps them do that. This is the interaction Hanji's research is trying to improve.

## What you keep

The canvas holds the exploration. The issue holds the commitment. The document holds the reasoning and the learning. Together they make the work easier to pick up again, by a person or by an agent with the appropriate access.

For setup, start with [[Desktop workspace]]. For Hanji's larger direction, read [[Mission and vision]].

---

# Using Hanji

Start with [[From idea to action]] to understand how the workspace fits together. The guides below explain setup and each surface in depth.

1. [[Quick start]] — choose the desktop preview or the existing-checkout path.
2. [[Desktop workspace]] — install the preview, create a workspace, and move between products.
3. [[Install Hanji]] — explicit setup for an existing checkout or server.
4. [[Think canvas]] — notes, shapes, tables, templates, workshops and agent activity.
5. [[Planning work]] — issues, agent mentions, project context and reviewing contributions.
6. [[Objectives and key results]] — the goal hierarchy and check-ins in Plan.
7. [[Reading and writing]] — pages, editing, search, history and organization in Document.
8. [[Workspace insights]] — contributions, trends, filters and the journal across products.
9. [[The conductor]] — one standing agent conversation across the workspace.
10. [[Mounts]] — connect your repositories and local folders.
11. [[Links and references]] — connect pages, issues, projects and canvases.
12. [[Comments]] — discuss a page and anchor feedback to its text.
13. [[Agents]] — scoped MCP tokens and agent proposals.
14. [[Proposals]] — review, merge or reject suggested edits.
15. [[Publish to the web]] — public HTML, Markdown mirrors and llms.txt.
16. [[On your tailnet]] — share a workspace through your own network.
17. [[Command reference]] — CLI commands, settings and environment variables.

Hanji’s app is an invited desktop preview. The handbook is public. The products
run on your machine or a server you operate; hosted workspace sync is not included.
Connect an agent only when you want one. Your provider account is separate.
