<!-- handbook/guide/install.md -->

---
title: Install Hanji
order: 10
description: Install the invited Mac preview, or run an existing source checkout.
---

# Install Hanji

Hanji runs today on a machine you own - the same way we run it ourselves, daily. The short version: install, `pnpm dev:web`, and the first visit walks you through everything on a welcome screen. This page keeps the explicit path - environment variables and CLI - for servers, scripts, and the people who like to see the wiring. Anything set by env always wins over what the welcome screen stored.

## Desktop preview: from download to workspace

The desktop preview is currently shared directly; no public binary release is
published. [The desktop setup guide](https://hanji.ink/start/) explains access,
installation and the first few minutes. Once you receive a preview archive:

1. Unzip it and read **Start here.html**. Use the build shared for your Mac.
2. Move **Hanji.app** into **Applications**, then open it there.
3. Choose **Create your workspace**. Existing workspace folders and team
   addresses have separate entry points on the same screen.
4. Name the workspace and choose Think, Plan and Document. All three start on;
   Settings can change the selection later.
5. Choose **Start fresh** to let Hanji prepare the selected products’ folders.
   Document includes an editable welcome page. **Bring existing content** asks
   for only the relevant Markdown, repository, tracker and canvas sources.
6. Set and confirm the owner's password, review the choices, then select
   **Create workspace**. The desktop signs this Mac in automatically.

**Quick setup help** opens inside onboarding, with guidance available even before
a workspace exists. Escape closes it and returns focus to its button.

The name, selected products and fresh/import choice survive a reload in this
browser tab. Passwords are never stored in that draft. Back and review links keep
in-memory choices. Setup errors remain visible and can be corrected or retried;
new folders and mounts roll back before the owner account is stored. Existing
files are preserved. New fresh-start folders live inside the data folder, with a
numbered suffix when an existing folder already uses the name.

![Choose a workspace and products](assets/onboarding-workspace.png)

![A final review before creation](assets/onboarding-review.png)

![The four setup stages](assets/onboarding-setup.gif)

Preview signing and notarization depend on the supplied build. If macOS cannot
verify it, confirm its source with the person sharing it and follow
[Apple’s guidance on opening apps safely](https://support.apple.com/102445).
The preview pack never changes Gatekeeper settings.

## Preparing a preview to share

Build the desktop bundle using `pnpm --filter desktop bundle`, then run:

```bash
bash apps/desktop/scripts/package-preview.sh /path/to/Hanji.app
```

The script creates a versioned, architecture-labeled ZIP and SHA-256 checksum
under `apps/desktop/dist/`. The archive includes Hanji.app, an Applications
shortcut and an offline Start here guide. It refuses to overwrite an existing
artifact. An optional second argument selects an output directory. It does not
publish a release, sign or notarize a build, or install it. Public distribution
still needs a release and the appropriate signing/notarization process.

## Before you start

You need a recent Node, `pnpm`, and `git`. One dependency, the SQLite driver, is built from source on install, so you also need a working C toolchain: the Xcode command-line tools on a Mac, or `build-essential` on Linux. That is a known rough edge, and smoothing it out is on the [[Where we are]].

## Get it running

```bash
# 1. install
pnpm install

# 2. point it at a data dir and set the front's secrets
export HANJI_DATA_DIR=~/.hanji
export HANJI_SESSION_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
export HANJI_OWNER_PASSWORD=choose-one

# 3. mount a repo you own (name, git url, mount path)
pnpm hanji add-mount notes git@github.com:you/notes.git notes

# 4. clone and index it
pnpm hanji sync

# 5. run the two surfaces
pnpm dev:web   # the human front at http://localhost:4100
pnpm dev:mcp   # the agent surface at http://localhost:4101/mcp
```

Open `http://localhost:4100`, sign in with the owner password you set, and your notes are there, rendered on cool neutral paper. That is the whole thing running.

<figure>
<img src="assets/login.png" alt="Hanji Document's sign-in card: the workspace mark, Hanji Document, the workspace's name, one sentence, and the Name and Password fields with Enter" class="w-25">
<figcaption>The front door. The owner leaves the name empty and types the owner password; people you add sign in with their own name and password. A link opened while signed out comes back to its page after sign-in.</figcaption>
</figure>

## The three secrets

| Variable | What it is |
|---|---|
| `HANJI_DATA_DIR` | Where Hanji keeps clones, disposable `index.db`, and durable `config.db` (accounts, grants, settings and comments). Back up `config.db`; it is not rebuilt from Git. |
| `HANJI_SESSION_SECRET` | The key that signs your login session. Any 32-byte hex string. |
| `HANJI_OWNER_PASSWORD` | The password for the single owner account, the one that reads and writes everything. |

Two more are optional. `HANJI_GITHUB_TOKEN` lets the propose path open real pull requests on a clone mount (a local mount's proposal opens none), and `HANJI_GIT_AUTHOR_NAME` with `HANJI_GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL` set the name on the owner's commits; without the variable, the name you set in Settings → People (Settings → General while the workspace has no people) is used, and with neither, Hanji Owner. See [[Agents]] for the first and [[Command reference]] for the rest.

Next, point Hanji at the repositories you actually want. Read [[Mounts]].

Product activation restores document visibility synchronously, including when WebKit has paused a hidden view. Content arrival uses a short finite animation without changing the document’s opacity or positioning context.

---

<!-- handbook/guide/links.md -->

---
title: Links and references
order: 32
description: How a page names an issue, a project, a board or another page, and who sees each link.
---

# Links and references

A workspace can hold pages, a tracker and boards. A double-bracket link in a page can name any of them, and every link is checked against the reader's own access.

## The forms

| You write | It names | It opens |
|---|---|---|
| `[[HNJ-12]]` | an issue in one of the workspace's trackers | the issue in Hanji Plan |
| `[[project:HNJ/onboarding]]` | a project in the tracker | nothing yet: the link shows its label |
| `[[board:boards/crit#9f2c]]` | a board, or one object on it | the board in Hanji Think, with that object selected |
| `[[Roadmap]]` or `[[Roadmap#Goals]]` | a page, by its title or its file name, with an optional heading | the page, scrolled to the heading |

The same forms work in an issue's `source:` field. A label after a bar chooses the words a reader sees: `[[board:boards/crit#9f2c|board note]]`.

A page written up from a board in Hanji Think ends with such a link, `From the board [[board:boards/crit#s1|Crit › Ideas]].` for a section and `From the board [[board:boards/crit|Crit]].` for a selection, labeled with the board's title and the section's name; a section's options in Think then offer **Open write-up** to a reader of that page. Any page that links a section that way counts as its write-up. See [[Think canvas]].

A key like `HNJ-12` names an issue only when the workspace holds a tracker with the prefix `HNJ` (a workspace can hold several trackers, each with its own prefix), so a page named `Q3-2026` stays a page. For a reader who cannot read that tracker, the key is page text too, the answer that reader would get with no tracker in the workspace. A title that holds a `#`, like `Sprint #12 retro`, also stays a page: Hanji tries the whole text as a title first, and reads the part after the first `#` as a heading only when that finds nothing.

## Who sees a link

A link opens only for a reader who can read what it names. For anyone else it shows as plain text, the same text a link to something missing shows, so a link never tells a reader that a hidden issue or page exists. In Document that text has a dotted underline, and pointing at it says what is missing from the link's own words: `No issue HNJ-999 in Hanji Work`, `No page named Roadmap`, `No board at boards/crit`.

## Cited by

At the foot of a page, **Cited by** lists the issues whose body or `source:` names that page, by title or file name, in any letter case, with or without a heading. A canceled issue is left out of the list; a done one stays. Each key shows the issue's title and status when you point at it. A reader sees the list only when they can read the tracker's mount. The tracker writes these links once its folder is registered as a work mount in the same data folder; see [[Mounts]]. On a tailnet, Hanji Plan signs in each person who holds view on the tracker's work mount, so an issue opens from this list, and from an issue link, for each of them; see [[On your tailnet]].

## From and Mentioned in

In Hanji Plan, an issue's **Related work** shows its source under **From** by name: a page by its title, a board by its title, and an object on it as the board's title, a `›` and the object's first line. A page source may also be written as `docs/plan.md`, the way Document shows a page's place. A source Plan cannot open for you shows as written, with a note that says which product did not find it. **Mentioned in** lists the pages that link the issue by its key, `[[HNJ-12]]`, by their titles, for a reader who may read them.

## Docs on a project

In Hanji Plan, a project group on a view's canvas lists under **Docs** the pages that cite the project, for a reader who may read them: a page that ends with `Documentation for the [[project:HNJ/<slug>|project]].` or `Status of the [[project:HNJ/<slug>|project]] on <date>.` is one. The owner's **Draft a doc** and **Draft a status** start a session that writes such a page in the chat and proposes it when the owner says so.

## When things move

Issue keys never change and are never used twice. Pages resolve by title or file name, so moving a page to another folder keeps its links. Renaming both the title and the file breaks the links to it: `tracker lint` reports the issue sources that no longer find a page, and `board-missing` for a source whose board or object is gone, and nothing rewrites the files that link to it.

Each product also works alone. With Document alone, issue, project and board links show their labels and Cited by is empty. With Plan alone, sources show as text. Without any app, every link is readable text in git.

Issue links and Cited by open Plan at the address in `HANJI_TRACKER_URL`, which is `http://127.0.0.1:4102` unless you set it, and board links open Think at `HANJI_THINK_URL`, `http://127.0.0.1:4104` unless you set it; see [[Command reference]]. A board link opens for a reader with view on that board, or on the whole mount of boards; see [[Permissions]]. A link to one object finds it once the board has written it to its files, at a Git checkpoint: until then, the link to a new sticky shows its label, and a deleted sticky's link still opens the board.

In a browser, each product's header offers the workspace's other tools you can open, Document, Plan and Think in that order, as links to their addresses in the same tab, with the one you are in marked (Plan shows them on their own row under the workspace name); a tool that is off, or one you cannot open, has no link, and a workspace of one tool shows none.

In a browser a link to a sibling product opens in the same tab, as a page link does: an issue link in a page, Open issue or a chip on a board, and Open write-up all leave the tab where they are. ⌘ with the click on a Mac, Ctrl elsewhere, or the middle button, opens a new one. A board sends the edits it still holds before it leaves, so nothing typed a moment before the click is lost, and Back returns to the board. A link that leaves the suite, a link card's Open link for one, keeps its new tab.

---

<!-- handbook/guide/mounts.md -->

---
title: Mounts
order: 20
description: Pointing Hanji at repositories, and keeping them in sync.
---

# Mounts

A **mount** is one git repository, or one folder inside it, brought into Hanji's tree. You can have many. Together they form the single knowledge base that people and agents read.

<figure><img src="assets/sidebar.png" alt="The sidebar: two mounts, their nested folders and pages, and a pending proposal card" class="w-50"><figcaption>Two mounts on the rail. Each is a repository; together they read as one collection.</figcaption></figure>

## Adding one

An empty workspace offers this right on its front page: mount a folder or clone a repository, no terminal involved. The welcome screen can connect your existing content, or prepare new local folders when you choose Start fresh. Its import path asks separately for Document pages, a Plan tracker and Think canvases. More folders can be added under Settings, Tools (below), or from the terminal. The CLI is the explicit path, and the only one with the full set of knobs:

```bash
pnpm hanji add-mount <name> <repoUrl> <mountPath> [subpath] [--suggest] [--local] [--kind pages|work|think]
```

- `name` is how you refer to the mount, and it is the token scope that grants access to it.
- `repoUrl` is any git URL Hanji can clone: an SSH remote, an HTTPS remote, or a local path.
- `mountPath` is where it lives in the tree, the first segment of every page's address.
- `subpath` is optional. Give it to mount only a folder of the repo, so the rest of the repository stays out of the knowledge base.
- `--local` mounts a folder on this machine in place: Hanji indexes its files where they are, and a save commits there without pushing. Hanji stores the folder's absolute path, so `.` works.
- `--kind` sets the mount's kind by hand; see Kinds of mount below.

```bash
# a whole repo
pnpm hanji add-mount notes git@github.com:you/notes.git notes

# only the docs/ folder of a larger repo
pnpm hanji add-mount handbook git@github.com:you/product.git handbook docs
```

An [Open Knowledge Format](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/open-knowledge-format) bundle mounts like any other repository, because that is all it is: Markdown concept documents on git, each with a `type` in its frontmatter. Hanji indexes every concept, keeps its frontmatter byte-for-byte, and serves the bundle to people and agents like the rest of your tree. Nothing to configure.

## Kinds of mount

Each mount has a kind, read from its files when you add it, and `add-mount` prints it:

- **pages** holds Markdown pages: everything above, and every mount added before kinds existed.
- **work** holds a tracker for Hanji Plan. Hanji knows it by its tracker file, `workspace.yml` at the root, with a `prefix:` line.
- **think** holds boards for Hanji Think. Each first-level folder that holds a `board.md` with Think's `id` and `version`, and a `nodes/` folder beside it, is one board, and Think serves it at `/b/<mountPath>/<folder>`.

A docs page that happens to be called `board.md` stays a page. `--kind pages`, `--kind work` or `--kind think` sets the kind by hand.

A mount added before kinds existed, or added by repository URL, is pages. To change it, remove the mount and add it again, with `--kind` when detection cannot see the kind.

Plan and think mounts are folders on this machine: add them with `--local`. Each product pulls its own folder, so a sync never resets a tracker commit that is still waiting to be pushed or a board checkpoint that stays on this machine. A workspace can register several trackers, each with a prefix of its own; a second tracker whose prefix is already registered is refused.

With several trackers, Hanji Plan serves them all: its rail lists the trackers you may view, an address names one by its prefix after the route word (`/v/HNJ/my-open`, `/okr/OPS`), an issue's address names it by its key (`/i/OPS-12`), and an address with no prefix opens the first tracker in the order Settings lists the mounts (for a person who may not view it, the first one they may view). Adding a tracker keeps the order the mounts had, so the first stays first. Each tracker keeps its own people and grants: a person sees the trackers whose work mount they may view and files into the ones they may edit, from Plan, from a page in Document or from a sticky in Think, each of which asks which tracker when there are two or more. The conductor's settings are set on the first tracker's Workspace settings; its `tracker` CLI acts on that tracker, and its tools reach every tracker the person may view or edit. A tracker folder that is not one of the workspace's work mounts starts no agent session in it.

<figure><img src="assets/work-trackers.png" alt="Plan's rail with two trackers, HNJ marked and OPS under it" class="w-50"><figcaption>Two trackers in one workspace: the rail switches between them.</figcaption></figure>

A tracker or a boards folder is added from Settings, under Tools, and a second tracker with **Add another tracker…** under Plan's row (an existing tracker folder, or a new one): turning Hanji Plan or Hanji Think on asks for the folder, an existing one or a new one made for you, and registers it as the mount. Turning a tool off keeps the mount, its folder and who can see it; turning it on again asks nothing. The CLI does the same with `add-mount` and `tools`.

A work or think mount for a tool that is off stays registered and keeps its people and rules; Mount access tags it "Plan is off" with the way to Tools, and `add-mount` says so. While a tool is off, every product shows a reference into it as plain text and offers no way into it: no issue link, Cited by link or issue action with Plan off, no page link or Docs with Document off, no board link with Think off. A Plan or Think you run by hand for such a workspace serves anyway and says at start that its tool is off.

Document lists, searches and syncs pages mounts only: a tracker's issue files and a board's node files never show in the sidebar, search or the digest. Activity shows them as the issues and boards they are, to a reader of the work or think mount.

A save, upload, move, delete, reorder or proposal into a work or think mount is refused: those files belong to Plan and Think, which check them before they write.

```bash
pnpm hanji add-mount work ~/trackers/design work --local    # mounted work at /work as work (local)
```

A folder that holds a single board at its root is refused, because a board is addressed by its folder: move the board into a folder of its own first (`git mv board.md nodes assets crit/`), commit, and add the mount again.

## Keeping in sync

Hanji reads from a local clone and serves from a local index. To pull the latest from a mount's remote and reindex, sync.

```bash
pnpm hanji sync       # fetch every pages mount and reindex what changed
pnpm hanji rebuild    # throw the index away and rebuild it from the clones
pnpm hanji list       # show every mount, its kind, and how many pages each pages mount holds
```

`rebuild` is safe to run any time. The index is a cache, so nothing you care about lives only there. If it ever looks wrong, rebuild it and it is correct again.

## Changes arrive on their own

Manual sync works, but a knowledge base should not need asking. Two mechanisms, both optional, both feeding the same sync:

**Push-to-sync.** Set `HANJI_WEBHOOK_SECRET` in the web front's environment, then add a webhook to the repository (GitHub: repo → Settings → Webhooks): payload URL `https://<your-hanji>/api/webhook/git`, content type JSON, the same secret. Every push to the mount's branch syncs the matching mount seconds later. Hanji answers deliveries immediately and does the git work in the background, so a slow clone never trips the sender's timeout. Deliveries are verified against the secret's signature; without the secret set, the endpoint does not exist.

**The poll loop.** Set `HANJI_POLL_SECONDS=300` and the web front syncs every pages mount on that interval. This is the mechanism for a tailnet, which a webhook cannot reach from the outside - see [[On your tailnet]] - and it also covers local mounts, picking up edits made outside Hanji entirely. A slow sync skips a beat, so syncs never stack; a failing one logs and tries again next round.

**The front syncs itself.** The web app freshens local mounts the moment attention arrives: switching back to the tab triggers a sync, and a quiet interval keeps checking while a page is open. A sync that finds nothing costs milliseconds - Hanji stats the tree and stops when nothing moved - so by the time you are looking, the page already shows what your agent just wrote. The byline says so: a small "checked just now" affix, with "sync failed - retry" when a mount cannot be read.

Any mix works: webhooks where the network allows, polling where it doesn't, `pnpm hanji sync` whenever you want it now.

## Direct and suggest mounts

By default a mount is **direct**: editors' edits in the front (the owner's, and anyone granted `read+write`) are written straight to git as commits. Pass `--suggest` and the mount becomes **suggest-only**: direct writes are refused, and every change has to arrive as a proposal instead.

Suggest mounts are for repositories where nothing should change without review, even from the owner. On a suggest mount Update reads Propose for everyone, editors and the owner included, agents alike, and every change waits in the same review card. See [[Proposals]].

Once your mounts are in place, read [[Reading and writing]] to use the front, or [[Agents]] to connect a coding agent.

---
title: Objectives and key results
order: 95
description: Read goals, their outcomes and the work behind their progress.
---

# Objectives and key results

Open **Objectives** in Plan's sidebar. The overview counts objectives, key results and results whose check-ins are due. Company goals group the objectives supporting them beneath a labeled branch. Objectives without a resolved company parent appear on their own.

![Company goals and their supporting objectives](assets/work-objectives.png)

Each objective separates its code, kind, owner and period from the title. Its progress stays in a dedicated summary. When a manual override differs from the calculated value, both numbers are identified. An unmeasured objective says **Not measured**; an empty one stays compact rather than drawing an empty progress bar.

Key results align in columns for the outcome, progress, confidence and check-in. Titles wrap so the full outcome remains readable. Confidence uses **On track**, **At risk**, **Off track** or **Not assessed**, alongside the existing semantic color. The check-in column combines age and **Update due**, without repeating the age in a warning badge. Completed binary key results no longer need check-ins and never show **Update due**. Unfinished binary results and metrics still become due after 14 days without a check-in; metrics retain this rule even at 100%, because their measure can recur.

Select a key result to expand its measurement, source, latest dated note and linked issues, projects and milestones. Focus the row and press Enter or Space to toggle it with the keyboard. Issue links open their issue pages.

![The measurement and linked work behind a key result](assets/work-objectives.gif)

The view reflows inside narrower windows, keeping the outcome and percentage readable together and placing confidence and check-in below. It supports light, dark and reduced-motion preferences.

Objective definitions, check-ins, linked-work progress and manual overrides read from the workspace's Markdown. The view uses the same calculated values as `tracker okr`.

The header’s **New issue** uses the workspace’s light primary button, matching **New canvas** in Think.

<!-- handbook/guide/on-your-tailnet.md -->

---
title: On your tailnet
order: 55
description: Run Hanji on a tailnet and let the tailnet sign people in.
---

# On your tailnet

The recommended way to share a Hanji instance with a team is not a domain, a
certificate, and a public endpoint. It is a [tailnet](https://tailscale.com):
the instance runs on one box, `tailscale serve` fronts it, and it never
touches the public internet. That sentence is the whole security posture, and
it is a sentence you can say to an administrator with a straight face.

Tailscale mode adds the part that makes it feel finished: the tailnet already
knows who is knocking, so Hanji stops asking.

## Turn it on

One variable, plus the serve command:

```bash
export HANJI_TAILSCALE_OWNER=you@github   # your own tailnet login
node_modules/.bin/next start -H 127.0.0.1 -p 4100
tailscale serve --bg 4100
```

Setting `HANJI_TAILSCALE_OWNER` does two things at once. It tells Hanji to
trust the identity headers `tailscale serve` attaches, and it names the
tailnet login that is the owner: you. Open the instance from any device on
your tailnet and you are simply in, as the owner, no password asked.

## Let people in

Everyone else maps through Settings → People. Open a person's sheet and link
their tailnet login in the Tailscale field. From then on, that identity signs
them in with no password. What they can see and propose is set by the grants
you gave them; the tailnet only says who they are. See [[Permissions]].

People starts with you: an **Owner** row with one field, Name. It goes on your commits and reads in bylines and History, in Hanji Plan's assignee list and History, and on your comments in Hanji Think. Commits you made before you set it read under it too: History at once, and a page's byline once the page is edited again or `hanji rebuild` runs (a byline indexed before this build holds no email to match). A name a person or an agent already uses is refused. With `HANJI_GIT_AUTHOR_NAME` set, the server's environment names you and the field is disabled.

<figure><img src="assets/person-sheet.png" alt="A person's sheet: their grants, and the Tailscale login field linking their tailnet identity" class="w-50"><figcaption>One person, one sheet: what they hold, and the tailnet identity that signs them in.</figcaption></figure>

An unlinked visitor is told plainly: the sign-in card names the tailnet
identity it saw and says the owner has not linked it yet, once tailscaled has
confirmed the login. The password form always works too: a linked login adds a
way to sign in and leaves passwords in place. Hanji Plan and Hanji Think show
the same card with the same sentence; off the tailnet, Plan's card points at
the computer's own address and Think's at the owner's access link, and a Think
session that ended says so first. On the tailnet the card links to the
product's tailnet address when `HANJI_TRACKER_URL` or `HANJI_THINK_URL` names
it, and otherwise says to ask the owner for it.

<figure><img src="assets/signed-out-work.png" alt="Hanji Plan's signed-out card: the mark, the product's name, a heading, one sentence and one link" class="w-50"><figcaption>One card in all three products: the mark, the product, why, and the one way forward.</figcaption></figure>

This is also how you invite someone from outside your team: share your node
with them in Tailscale, add them as a person, link their login.

## Hanji Plan on the tailnet

Hanji Plan signs people in the same way. Build it, start it with the same owner and the same data folder as Document, and serve it on a second port:

```bash
export HANJI_TAILSCALE_OWNER=you@github   # the same login as Write's
export HANJI_DATA_DIR=~/.hanji            # the same folder as Write's
export TRACKER_WORKSPACE=/path/to/tracker  # only for a tracker that is not registered as a work mount; registered ones are served from the data folder
pnpm --filter tracker-web build           # again after each update of Hanji
pnpm --filter tracker-web start           # serves 127.0.0.1:4102
tailscale serve --bg --https=8443 4102
```

With several trackers registered, Plan serves them all from that one port: each person reaches the trackers whose work mount they may view, by its prefix in the address.

Plan reads people and grants from that data folder, so Document's server does not need to run. To let your team in:

1. Register the tracker as a mount of the workspace, in its own folder: `pnpm hanji add-mount work /path/to/tracker work --local`. Hanji finds the tracker file (`workspace.yml`) and records the mount as kind work. The tracker's database keeps working, since it is keyed by the tracker's prefix and folder.
2. In Document, under Settings → People, add each teammate, link their tailnet login, and make them a Viewer or an Editor of the work mount.
3. For each teammate who edits, add their Document user name under `people:` in the tracker file, and commit it:

```yaml
people:
  ada: Ada, design lead
  remy: Remy, designer
```

| On the work mount | In Hanji Plan |
|---|---|
| no access | every address answers 404, and the reply names nothing about the tracker |
| Viewer | views, issues, projects, proposals and sessions |
| Editor, with a `people:` entry | also edits issues, projects and views, comments, and files an issue from a page in Document or from a sticky in Think, with their name on each commit |
| Editor, without one | views only; each edit answers with the entry to add |

The owner needs no `people:` entry to file an issue from a page in Document or from a sticky in Think.

Actions that let an agent run code on this machine stay with the owner: Allow on a permission, a message to a session, Open in Ghostty, starting the conductor, a comment sent to an agent, a comment on an issue whose ask or build is waiting, asking for a build, Workspace settings, starting the session host, and applying or discarding a proposal. A teammate who tries one is told so. Deny and Stop only stop work, so a teammate with edit and a `people:` entry can use them. A write sent from a page on another site is refused. A session's log shows the folders and commands its agent used on the owner's machine, so anyone who can view sessions sees them.

A private tracker belongs to a private workspace: start its Plan server with its own `HANJI_DATA_DIR`. A tracker served from a folder that is not a registered work mount of the data folder opens for the owner only.

### Links between the products

Each product links to the others through three addresses: `HANJI_KB_URL` (Document, default `http://127.0.0.1:4100`), `HANJI_TRACKER_URL` (Plan, default `http://127.0.0.1:4102`) and `HANJI_THINK_URL` (Think, default `http://127.0.0.1:4104`). The defaults open the visitor's own machine, which suits one person on localhost. On a tailnet, set all three to their `tailscale serve` addresses on every product server, so a teammate who follows "Cited by" from a Document page opens Plan on your machine:

```bash
export HANJI_KB_URL=https://mac.tailnet.ts.net
export HANJI_TRACKER_URL=https://mac.tailnet.ts.net:8443
export HANJI_THINK_URL=https://mac.tailnet.ts.net:8444
```

A board link in a Document page (`[[board:boards/crit#9f2c]]`) and an issue's **From** link in Plan open Think at `HANJI_THINK_URL`.

Think opens a page it wrote up, and a proposal it made, in Document at `HANJI_KB_URL`.

The three addresses also decide which requests the tailnet login signs in. In tailnet mode, Document, Plan and Think trust the `Tailscale-User-Login` header only on a request whose `Host` is this machine's loopback address (`127.0.0.1`, `localhost` or `[::1]`, on any port), which covers requests made on this machine, or the host name of one of the three addresses. `tailscale serve` passes the tailnet name as the `Host` when it forwards a request, which is why one of the three addresses must name it. Host names compare without the port and without regard to letter case. A web page open in a browser on this machine can point its own domain at 127.0.0.1 and send a login header of its own, but it cannot change the `Host` that its own domain gives it, so it cannot sign itself in as the owner. A request with any other `Host` gets no sign-in from the header: Plan and Think answer 403, and Document treats the visitor as anonymous.

If a sign-in that worked before now answers 403 in Plan, or shows the login page in Document, the product addresses are not set to the `tailscale serve` names. Set all three as shown above on every product server and restart each one.

## Hanji Think on the tailnet

Hanji Think signs people in the same way. Start it with the same owner and the same data folder, with its own address set, and serve it on a third port:

```bash
export HANJI_TAILSCALE_OWNER=you@github   # the same login as Write's
export HANJI_DATA_DIR=~/.hanji            # the same folder as Write's
export HANJI_THINK_URL=https://mac.tailnet.ts.net:8444
node scripts/whiteboard-build.mjs
node --import tsx packages/whiteboard/src/main.ts --port 4104
tailscale serve --bg --https=8444 4104
```

Think admits the tailnet name as a `Host` when any one of the three product addresses names it, so the three set as above are enough. If none of the three names the tailnet host, Think answers 403 to every request through the proxy. Register the folder of boards as a think mount, `pnpm hanji add-mount boards /path/to/boards boards --local --kind think`, and give each teammate a grant on it in Settings → People, on the whole mount or on one board folder:

| On the think mount | In Hanji Think |
|---|---|
| no access | every address of that board answers 404, the same as for a board that does not exist |
| Viewer | opens the board and follows its links |
| Commenter | also comments and reacts |
| Editor | also edits |

Off the tailnet, the owner's access link, printed by the launcher, opens Think; teammates sign in on the tailnet only. Agents hold their own keys (`key --agent <handle>`), which act with the owner's access. A write sent from a page on another site is refused, and a grant removed ends an open board within a second; the board page then says that access ended and asks to reload or open a new access link.

## The contract

The headers are trustworthy when two conditions hold. First, the app binds
`127.0.0.1`, as above, so `tailscale serve` and requests from this machine are
the only ways in, and `tailscale serve` strips any inbound `Tailscale-User-*`
headers and sets its own. If the app is reachable any other way, anyone on that
path can type the header themselves, and `HANJI_TAILSCALE_OWNER` must stay
unset. Second, the request's `Host` names
this machine's loopback address or one of the three product addresses, which
keeps a web page open on this machine from sending a header of its own, as
the section on links between the products describes. Hanji checks the second
condition on every request, and will never turn this mode on by itself.

Two more facts. Signing out on a tailnet clears the session cookie, and the next
request signs you in again through the header, because the tailnet still knows
who you are. And agents are untouched by all of this. The MCP surface stays
bearer-token only, and a tailnet identity never grants an agent anything.

`tailscale serve` adds the identity headers to every request from your
machine, including a request that another website makes your browser send.
Document answers such a request with 403: every route that changes something
accepts it only from Document's own pages, judged by the browser's
`Sec-Fetch-Site` and `Origin` headers. Scripts and the git webhook send
neither header and keep working. A proxy in front of Document must pass the
browser's original `Host` header or set `X-Forwarded-Host`, which
`tailscale serve` does. With neither, Document answers every save with 403.

## Belt and suspenders: ask tailscaled itself

The contract above is a deployment shape. If you want the instance to verify
it rather than assume it, set one more variable:

```bash
export HANJI_TAILSCALE_WHOIS=1
```

On every header sign-in, Hanji now asks the local tailscaled who owns the
connecting address (`tailscale whois`, one lookup per address per minute) and
refuses the header unless the answers match. A forged header alone no longer
signs anyone in; it would take tailscaled itself vouching for the forger's
address, which the tailnet does not do. The check needs the `tailscale` CLI
on the PATH of the user running Hanji; point `HANJI_TAILSCALE_BIN` at the
binary when it lives elsewhere (on a Mac,
`/Applications/Tailscale.app/Contents/MacOS/Tailscale`). When in doubt, turn
it on: the cost is one process spawn per new visitor address, and the failure
mode is a login page instead of a wrongly trusted header.

## Why this is not SSO

It is better, for the case it covers. On a tailnet you do not integrate an
identity provider; you already have one, and it is the network itself.
Single sign-on for organizations that live behind Okta or Google Workspace
remains where [[Where we are]] puts it: the paid seam, later. This mode is
for the team that wants the writing surface working today, with nobody
typing passwords, on infrastructure they already trust.

---

<!-- handbook/guide/planning-work.md -->

---
title: Planning work
order: 27
description: Create clear tasks, work with agents and keep a project understandable in Plan.
---

# Planning work

Plan gives work a place, an owner and a next step. People and configured agents work on the same issues and projects; the interface keeps the task and its discussion together.

This guide uses a fictional **First mile** project. Ada and Noor have decided to try an editable starter project before asking a new teammate to configure their own workspace. [[From idea to action]] shows where that decision began.

## Create a task someone can act on

Open Plan and select **New issue**. Give the task a clear title and describe the change you want, including what will count as ready. Set its project, assignee, status and priority as appropriate. Add dependencies when one task needs another to finish first.

For First mile, the task is **Create the editable starter project**. Its completion criteria are concrete: one clear first task, editable and removable sample content, and separation from imported work.

![A fictional starter-project issue, with its decision, criteria and related work](assets/public-plan-issue.png)

An issue can also start from selected notes in Think or a passage in Document. [[Links and references]] describes supported references between the surfaces.

## Ask an agent about a specific task

With the agent and session host configured, mention its handle in an issue comment. The built-in handles are **@claude** and **@gpt**; availability depends on the agents configured for your workspace.

For example:

> @claude clarify the acceptance criteria for this task and suggest a follow-up to test the first session.

The focused request includes the issue, its discussion and relevant project context. It helps the agent work from a concrete brief rather than making every task part of a single growing conversation. The reply stays attached to the work. A workspace thread can also ask one or more configured agents by mentioning their handles.

An agent's response is a contribution to review. Check the criteria, confirm the scope and decide which suggested follow-up work to keep. A response saying a task is ready is not evidence that the result has been tested.

## Ask the conductor about the wider project

Open the conductor when the question crosses tasks or surfaces. You might ask:

> What changed in First mile, and what should we review before the next test?

The conductor carries the current issue or view into the conversation. Within the available rights and tools, it can read relevant work, help organize tasks and make supported changes. It can also work with connected pages and canvases. [[The conductor]] explains context, approvals and Undo. [[Agents]] explains the separate provider setup and access boundaries.

## Choose the view that fits the question

Use the list for scanning tasks and their fields, the board for work by status, and the canvas for the arrangement and relationships of work. These are views of the same issues, rather than separate copies to keep in sync.

For goals and the evidence behind them, use [[Objectives and key results]]. Link the work that supports a goal and keep check-ins current where they are needed.

## Review changes and keep the reasoning

Read the task and its discussion after an agent contributes. Use history to understand changes, and record decisions that someone will need later in Document. Issues and projects are file-backed work with Git history. Workspace configuration and agent sessions have their own durable data, so back them up alongside repositories. The current preview does not provide hosted workspace sync.

Continue with [[Workspace insights]] to see recorded contributions across products, or [[Permissions]] to understand what each person and agent may access.

<!-- handbook/guide/proposals.md -->

---
title: Proposals
order: 45
description: Agents propose. You review the diff and merge, right in the front.
---

# Proposals

This is the page where Hanji stops being a wiki and becomes the thing it was built to be. An agent never edits your pages in place. It proposes a change, the proposal lands in the front, and you decide. The whole loop runs over git, and you never have to see that.

## The loop

1. An agent with `read+propose` scope calls `hanji_propose` (see [[Agents]]). Behind the scenes that becomes a `hanji/*` branch carrying one commit with the agent's change: on a clone mount, pushed to the mount's remote; on a local mount, a branch of your own repository.
2. A card appears in the sidebar, under the search box: how many proposals are waiting, and **Review**. It exists only while something waits; at zero the sidebar stays pure content. The count is cheap to compute, and it refreshes whenever a mount is synced or a proposal is made, merged or rejected.
3. Open the proposal. You get the title the agent gave it, who proposed it, which page it touches, its weight (+added/−removed), and a line diff: green for what it adds, red for what it removes. If the agent left a self-review note on the proposal, it sits beside the diff - the agent telling you where it is confident and where it is not, before you read a line. The queue itself reads like a triage view: each row carries the note, the diff's weight, and how long it has waited.
4. Press **Merge** or **Reject**. That is the entire ceremony.

A proposal the conductor wrote shows as a card in its panel in Hanji Document, Hanji Plan and Hanji Think, linking to the review in Hanji Plan, where Apply and Discard live; a card from a teammate's conversation says whose it was.

<figure><img src="assets/proposal-review.png" alt="A proposal open for review: title, proposer, the line diff, and Reject and Merge buttons"><figcaption>An agent's proposal, waiting. The diff is the whole conversation.</figcaption></figure>

<figure><img src="assets/merge.gif" alt="Opening a pending proposal, pressing Merge, and landing on the merged page with the agent's byline"><figcaption>Merge lands it: the page updates, and the byline says who really wrote it.</figcaption></figure>

## People propose too

Agents are not the only ones held to review. Mount a repository with `--suggest` and the human front follows the same rule: the editor works exactly as everywhere else, but **Update becomes Propose**, and pressing it opens a branch instead of committing. The proposal lands in the same card, gets the same diff, and waits for the same Merge. One review ceremony for every writer, whatever species they are.

## What Merge does

Merge lands the proposal on the page: a merge commit on the base branch, the proposal branch deleted, the page and the search index updated immediately. The agent's own commit survives in history with its name on it, so `git blame` a year from now still tells the truth about who wrote what.

On a clone mount the merge is pushed to the mount's remote. On a local mount the merge is a commit in your own repository, and the base branch moves forward in one of two ways. When the base is checked out in your folder, or in another worktree of yours, Hanji fast-forwards it there, which needs that worktree to hold no uncommitted edits to tracked files; with edits, Merge says "commit or stash your edits first" and nothing moves (an untracked file does not block). When the base is checked out nowhere (your folder on another branch, or at an older commit), Hanji moves the branch alone and leaves your files and your checked-out branch as they are; the page shows once you check the base out again. While you rebase or bisect the base, or when it moved during the merge, Merge says to press it again once the folder is settled, and nothing moves. A proposal that changes files outside the mount's folder (a branch made by hand, say) is not merged from Hanji, since Review shows the mount's part only. Nothing is pushed: push the merge as you push your own commits.

## What Reject does

Reject deletes the branch, and keeps the record. Who refused what, and when, is written down; the proposal's tip commit survives under a kept ref, `refs/hanji/rejected/<name>`, in the clone or in your own repository on a local mount, so the agent's diff never silently ceases to exist (`git branch hanji/<name> refs/hanji/rejected/<name>` brings it back). On a local mount, a proposal you have checked out in a worktree is not rejected until you switch that worktree to another branch. The page itself never knew it was threatened, and rejections appear on the Activity page for the owner - a refusal is a decision, and decisions deserve a trace.

## When the page moved underneath

If someone edited the page after the agent proposed, the two versions may no longer merge cleanly. Hanji checks before you do anything: the proposal opens with a warning and Merge is disabled. There is no conflict-resolution screen, on purpose. The honest move is to ask the agent to re-propose from the current page, or reject. A merge you have to untangle by hand defeats the point of reviewing calmly.

## The honest notes

- The review surface is owner-only. Agents can propose all day; only you merge.
- A proposal is a branch of the mount's repository, nothing more: on a clone mount a branch of its remote, on a local mount a branch of your own. There is no separate proposal database to back up or migrate. Walk away and the proposals walk with the repo.
- On a local mount, a proposal is a branch of your own repository, `hanji/<title>-<hex>`, made in a temporary worktree under the data folder: your checked-out branch, index and edits are not touched, nothing is fetched or pushed, and no pull request is opened. The `hanji/` branch namespace is Hanji's: a branch of yours named that way is read as a proposal while its tip is not on the base.
- One page per proposal in this version, which is exactly what `hanji_propose` produces.
- An agent can attach a self-review note to a proposal (what it is confident about, what it is not). The note rides the proposal's commit body and shows with the diff - read it before the diff, it usually tells you where to look.

Read [[Agents]] for minting the token that can propose, and [[Permissions]] for the scopes behind it.

---

<!-- handbook/guide/publish.md -->

---
title: Publish to the web
order: 48
description: One command turns everything open-to-everyone into a website, llms.txt included.
---

# Publish to the web

Some of what a team writes deserves an audience: the docs, the handbook, the
pages you would happily show a customer. Hanji publishes exactly the content
you have opened to everyone - and nothing else. The lock decides what goes;
the exporter never widens it.

The site you are reading right now was made this way.

## Choose, then publish

```bash
# 1. open what should be public (a mount, or just a folder)
pnpm hanji rule handbook everyone-read

# 2. render it
pnpm hanji export ./site
```

`./site` is now a complete static website in Hanji's look: your sidebar, your
reading order and dark mode. A small inline script remembers the theme choice;
reading and navigation also work without JavaScript. On a phone, Browse handbook
opens a native collapsible navigation panel so the article stays near the top;
a Skip to content link supports keyboard navigation. Beside every HTML page sits the
same page as plain Markdown, plus `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt` at the root -
so the agents reading the open web get your writing as text, not scraped
pixels.

## Put it on GitHub Pages

```bash
cd site
git init -b main && git add -A && git commit -m "Published with Hanji"
git remote add origin git@github.com:you/docs.git
git push origin main
# then: repository Settings → Pages → deploy from main
```

Publishing again is the same two commands: `hanji export` straight into that
clone (it cleans its own output and leaves `.git` alone), commit, push.

## Make it yours

A few optional settings shape the published site, set once from the CLI:

```bash
pnpm hanji set export_home_url https://your.site/     # the crumb's way home
pnpm hanji set export_home_label YourSite
pnpm hanji set export_site_label Handbook             # the crumb's right side
pnpm hanji set export_edit_base_url https://github.com/you/repo/edit/main/docs
```

With an edit base set, every published page ends with a quiet **suggest an
edit** link straight into your repository's web editor - a reader spots a
typo, clicks, and a pull request is two clicks away. The cheapest
contribution funnel there is.

## As an OKF bundle

Add `--okf` and the export is also an [Open Knowledge Format](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/open-knowledge-format) bundle, the vendor-neutral Markdown-on-git shape other agent tools read:

```bash
pnpm hanji export ./bundle --okf
```

Every page ships as a concept document with a `type` in its frontmatter (`Page` by default; a page that sets its own `type:` keeps it), the reserved `index.md` files carry no frontmatter, and the bundle root declares `okf_version`. The static site and `llms.txt` still ride along. Your source in git is untouched, the OKF shaping happens only in the copy on disk.

## What stays private

Everything without an everyone rule. A restricted folder inside an open mount
stays dark, its pages and even its images never leave the building. If
nothing is open at all, the exporter refuses loudly rather than shipping an
empty site - you will never publish by accident.


## This handbook’s publication

Maintainers can export only the handbook from an isolated publication state:

```bash
node --import tsx scripts/export-handbook.mjs /path/to/docs-artifact-checkout
node scripts/check-handbook-export.mjs /path/to/docs-artifact-checkout
```

This uses `docs/handbook` as the only mount. It does not change the rules of a
live workspace, copy other mounts or push a repository. Review the exported
HTML, assets and Markdown mirrors before committing the artifact. The marketing
site and this handbook have separate GitHub Pages deployments.

## The published reading experience

![The redesigned public handbook, with product entry cards, guide navigation and an on-page outline](assets/published-handbook.png)

The HTML export includes grouped navigation, a page-title finder and an on-page outline with stable section links. Previous and next links follow the exported navigation order. Each page links to its Markdown source. The page finder filters only titles and sections already present in the public navigation; it does not query the live workspace or index private content.

On smaller screens, guide navigation and the outline use native collapsible panels. Reading, navigation, section links and Markdown links work without JavaScript. JavaScript adds the title finder and explicit theme controls; without it the palette follows the system.

<figure>
<img src="assets/published-guide-mobile.png" alt="A published guide on a phone, with collapsed navigation and an on-page outline" class="w-50">
<figcaption>On a phone, navigation stays out of the reading path until you open it.</figcaption>
</figure>

<!-- handbook/guide/reading-and-writing.md -->

---
title: Reading and writing
order: 30
description: The human front: reading, editing, history, and new pages.
---

# Reading and writing

Everything here happens at `http://localhost:4100`, after you sign in. It is meant to feel like an editorial tool, not a git client. The owner and anyone granted `read+write` write straight to git; a contributor's Update reads Propose and lands in review (see [[Permissions]]).

## Settings

Settings is the owner's, under the workspace menu in a browser (in the app, under the title bar's gear), and it is the workspace's page rather than Document's: it keeps the `/kb/settings` address, which the app's gear and the links in Plan and Think reach, and draws without Document's sidebar, search, tree or conductor, under one row with a **Back** control that returns to the page you came from; the Activity journal (`/kb/activity`) is drawn the same way, with a product filter in its address when a product's link opened it. **General** holds the workspace's name, logo (drawn by the app's title bar seal and the tab's icon; no product draws a mark inside its own chrome), working mode, and the owner's name while the workspace has no people; **Tools**, **People** and **Mount access** are described in their own guides. **Appearance** holds the conductor’s shape and motion choices (see [[The conductor]]) and one color, the accent, near black unless you pick another. Document draws it as the current page's row, the text selection, the primary button, the focus ring and the text of its links, which inside a page are always underlined. Plan draws the same color on its own paper and updates open pages when the accent changes, including when you return from Settings. Think reads it the next time it loads. The page shows a pick at once, Save keeps it, and Reset returns to the default. When a color is too light or too dark to read where it is drawn (on the paper, the sheet, the recessed fields or the accent's light tints behind the current item, search hits and chips), Hanji corrects the role that failed, whether the fill, the link text, the button labels or the focus ring, and a line under the picker names it, for light and for dark. Light and dark follow your system. The three products and desktop shell share one slightly cool neutral palette, so the accent is the one color that changes between workspaces. What is Document's own sits under the **Document** tab: **Reading** (the font of the pages you read and write, the content width and the text size; titles and the rest of Document keep Newsreader), the sidebar's folding, and search (the alias page and the query log).

![The Accent control in Settings](assets/settings-appearance.png)

## Reading

Pages open on cool neutral paper, set in a serif for long reading. Document, Plan and Think share sidebar typography and spacing: compact section labels, 12px navigation rows, and search fields capped at 264px while the rail widens. Their Search… placeholder, glyph, border, colors and shortcut badge come from the same shared control styles. Edit and Save shortcuts inherit the button’s theme color. The sidebar on the left is your mounts and their folders, nested and collapsible, and it expands to show where you are. Mounts have full-height 33px rows and full-row hover targets. Collapsed mounts sit close together; expanded trees keep extra space after their children. Mount and folder carets use the same size and shape; mount children start one level below their mount. Folder arrows and document rows reserve the same disclosure column: sibling labels align, each child level moves 16px to the right, and quiet branch guides connect nested content to its parent. The selected document keeps that indentation. A breadcrumb across the top tells you the path, collapsing its middle on deep pages so it never runs off the screen. Wikilinks, written `[[by title]]`, resolve to the page they name, and only to pages you are allowed to open.

![Document hierarchy with aligned labels and branch guides](assets/document-sidebar-hierarchy.png)

Selecting a run of prose raises a small bar over it, and the text stays selected while the bar is up. **Copy** puts the selection on your clipboard twice over - as rich text for anywhere that takes it, and as real Markdown for anywhere that does not - so a paragraph pasted into another editor arrives with its headings, lists, tables, and code fences intact, and pasted into a plain text field arrives as the Markdown that made it. `⌘C` works exactly as it always did; the button is just the one that also carries the Markdown. **Comment** is another thing a selection can mean, and so is **Issue** when you can file work into the workspace's tracker; each is a deliberate press. See [[Comments]].

## Search

`⌘K` opens the palette. Before you type it offers the pages you changed most recently. The full search runs from the first character you type; from the second, matching titles answer ahead of it, because a title is the fast answer and a one-character prefix is the most expensive question the index can be asked. The two lists are one list: titles at the top, no page listed twice, each row carrying the page's title, the heading the match sits under, and the passage itself. Arrow keys move, Enter opens the row you are on, and `⌘Enter` takes the whole query to the results page.

The title tier is deliberately workspace-wide. It is the fast answer to "what is that page called", so it looks across every pages mount you can read, and it ignores the mount or path filter the rest of the search obeys.

<figure>
<img src="assets/search.gif" alt="The search palette opening with ⌘K, results ranking as the query is typed, and Enter opening a page">
<figcaption>⌘K, a few letters, Enter. The keyboard the whole way.</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure>
<img src="assets/search-palette.png" alt="The search palette with a title tier above ranked results, each showing its heading path and matching passage">
<figcaption>Titles first, then the passage that matched, with the heading it lives under.</figcaption>
</figure>

`/kb/search` is where you dig. It answers with exact counts rather than fast ones, twenty results to a page, grouped per page, with up to two passages under each and a third named on one line. The headline counts the pages that hold any of your words; a mount chip counts the pages in that mount that hold every one of them, and when those two numbers differ the page says so beneath the chips rather than leaving you to wonder. Words that matched nothing you can read are named under the count, along with the pages whose titles come closest, from anywhere you can read rather than from the mount a chip has narrowed you to, and the line says so. Paging stops at the 500th match, which is as deep as the pool goes, and says so instead of offering a page that would come back empty. A link into a page that is no longer there - a stale `?o=`, a bookmark into a result set that has since shrunk - says "No results on this page." rather than claiming nothing matched, and keeps its Previous link back to the results that exist. Narrow rather than page: a mount chip, or a filter inside the query.

A query can carry filters: `mount:handbook`, `path:notes/2026` (`in:` is the same thing), `title:release`, `-draft` to push a word away, and a phrase in quotes for words that must sit together. A `mount:` inside the query narrows the search itself, while the chip row follows the mount filter in the URL, so the two can say different things and each still describes what it did.

Opening a result lands you on the match. The page scrolls to the block that matched, that block wears a brief wash which fades on your first scroll, and the words that matched stay marked while you read. Where an alias class ties two spellings together, an English query marks the Korean word it actually found, and the other way round. Press Edit and both marks step aside; Escape back to reading brings the landing back.

### Aliases, so one word finds the other

A team writes 오퍼월 in one page and offerwall in the next, and search should not care which one you typed. Point Settings at one page in the library, named by its mount and then its page path (`notes/search-aliases.md`), and that page configures it:

```markdown
오퍼월 = offerwall, offer wall
정산 = settlement, payout
```

The mount goes by its name, which is not always the spelling in the address bar: a mount named `notes` that reads `/kb/p/team-notes/…` is `notes` here. Settings takes either spelling and saves the name, because that is the one search looks up. Any term in a class finds the pages that use the others. A table row with one term per cell is the same thing as a `=` line, so a class can live in a table with a heading row above it. Lines that share a term merge, so `a = b` and `b = c` become one class of three. A class holds up to 8 terms and a page up to 500 classes; entries past either cap are dropped, and Settings says how many went and names the first. A line that is not a class is skipped, and emptying the field turns aliases off. The list is a page like any other, which means the vocabulary of your search has history, review, and an author.

### The log of what people searched for

Hanji keeps the searches this workspace ran: the query as it was typed, the words it resolved to, how many results came back, how long it took, and which result was opened. No name is stored with a row, and nothing leaves the machine. The log lives beside your settings rather than in the index, so an entry outlives the page it names, and it keeps the last 10,000 searches; on a shared workspace, everyone's queries land in that one log. The switch in Settings turns it off, clicks included.

### When search says it is indexing

The index is a cache, and a change to its format empties it until it has been re-derived from the pages themselves. While that is true, the palette and the results page say the index is being built rather than dressing an empty answer as an answer. Settings has **Rebuild the index** for exactly that, owner only: it re-derives everything from stored page content, reports progress the way a first sync does, and takes minutes on a large library. One rebuild runs at a time, and the line above the button says where the index stands: that it is being checked, that it is in step with your pages, that it needs rebuilding and how many problems the check found, or that the check could not be run at all and why. The problems themselves are raw counts of rows against rows, so they sit behind **What the check found** rather than in the sentence.

## Writing

Editing is deliberate, and it is one gesture.

1. Press **Edit**, or `⌘E`. The page becomes editable in place, on the same measure you were reading, at the same scroll position - the header bar keeps its breadcrumb and simply swaps its buttons for **Discard** and **Update**.
2. Change what you came to change. It is a real editor: Markdown shortcuts, a slash menu to insert, tables with handles, task lists, images, embeds, and emoji (the toolbar's picker, or type `:` and a few letters).
3. Press **Update**. Hanji writes a single commit behind the scenes, with a clean message, and drops you back into reading.

The header bar stays with you: back and forward, the breadcrumb, and the page's actions stick to the top of the view, so a long page never scrolls away from its own controls. A hairline appears under it once the prose is running beneath, and is gone again at the top of the page.

### Line breaks, and tables

`⇧Enter` puts a line break inside the block you are in rather than starting a new one. Inside a table cell, plain **Enter** means the same thing, because a cell is one line and has nothing to split. A break is written to the file as `<br>` - the only spelling a table row can carry, and the one Hanji uses everywhere so that a break survives being moved from a paragraph into a cell and back.

That is also as far as a list in a cell goes: broken lines, each with its own dash. Markdown tables hold inline content only, so a real bullet list cannot live in a cell in any tool that writes Markdown - what you get is the lines, correctly broken, and the dashes you typed are left exactly as you typed them.

### Highlights

Highlight a phrase the way you would bold one: select it and press `⌘⇧H`, pick a swatch from the selection bubble or the bottom toolbar, or simply type `==like this==`. There are four colours - a default yellow, then blue, green, and pink - and pressing the swatch a highlight already wears takes it off again.

What lands in the file is worth knowing, because it is your file. The default colour writes `==the phrase==`, the portable spelling every other Markdown tool understands. A chosen colour has to write `<mark class="hl-blue">the phrase</mark>`, because standard Markdown has no way to name a colour. So the common case stays clean Markdown, and colour costs you portability only when you ask for one. Both read back as the same highlight, in the page and in the editor alike.

If you changed nothing, nothing is committed. There is no draft state to babysit, and no save button that lies. And because edits are byte-fidelity, the commit for a one-word fix is a one-line diff. See [[Byte-fidelity]].

<figure><img src="assets/edit-update.gif" alt="The whole editing gesture: Edit, a line typed in place, Update, and the fresh byline"><figcaption>The whole gesture: Edit, change, Update. One commit happened behind it.</figcaption></figure>

<figure><img src="assets/input-rules.gif" alt="Markdown shortcuts converting live: hashes into a heading, stars into bold, a dash into a list"><figcaption>Markdown as you type: hashes make headings, stars make bold, a dash starts a list.</figcaption></figure>

<figure><img src="assets/editor-toolbar.png" alt="The editor's floating bottom toolbar: format marks, block types, the four highlight swatches, and the inserts"><figcaption>The chrome of edit mode: the header bar you were already reading under, and this one floating bar.</figcaption></figure>

<figure><img src="assets/slash-menu.png" alt="The slash menu open in the editor, offering Code, Image, Video, Embed, and Table"><figcaption>Type a slash on a fresh line to insert.</figcaption></figure>

The slash menu offers Heading 1, Heading 2, Heading 3, Bulleted list, Numbered list and Quote, the same blocks as the toolbar, then Code, Image, Video, Embed and Table. Type a few letters of any word to narrow it: `/list` finds both lists. When nothing matches, the menu stays open on **No matches**. While you select text, the selection bubble carries the formatting and the bottom toolbar is hidden, and the line you are typing stays above the toolbar as the page scrolls.

## Fresh by the time you look

A page you are reading keeps itself current. While its tab is visible it checks itself every seven seconds, and when anyone changed it meanwhile - another editor pressing Update in the app, or an agent editing the underlying files - the page refreshes in place, quietly; switching back to the tab is enough to catch up. A one-line note says it happened, naming the page that moved, with a link straight to it when the change was somewhere else, or pointing at the Activity page when several moved at once. That includes the pictures: replacing an image counts as a change even though no prose moved, and the new picture arrives rather than the one your browser had already cached; no note for that, since there is no page to name and nothing for one to point at. When someone else has the page open in their editor, "Remy is editing" sits beside the byline, so you know a change is coming before it lands. The byline carries the trust surface: "checked just now" or "checked 4m ago" - when the index last agreed with the files, a different claim than the page's own "updated", which is about content - ticking as you read, with a quiet retry when a sync fails. Silence means nothing changed; nothing here ever interrupts.

## When two edits collide

Hanji notices if the page changed underneath you, and it never makes you throw your edits away to deal with it. While your editor is open, the page checks itself every seven seconds, and a change raises only a quiet line, not an alarm: "Remy changed this page. It will merge when you save." If the two edits fold together cleanly and you have not touched the keyboard for a few seconds, they stop waiting: their change is merged into what you are writing right then, your cursor goes back where it was, and a line tells you whose edit arrived. Touch the keyboard while that is being worked out and it is abandoned, to be tried again the next time you pause. The line names the other hand where the name is honest (the last committer, on a git-backed mount) and says "This page changed" on a plain folder. If someone else is editing at the same moment, a second line says so: "Remy is also editing this page. Edits merge when you save." There is no lock and no take-over; the merge waits until you save. As you type, your draft is kept in the browser too, so a reload or a closed tab loses nothing.

When you press Update and the page has moved, Hanji tries to fold the two edits together. Most of the time they touch different parts (someone fixed a link at the foot of the page while you rewrote the top), and the fold is clean: your work and theirs both land in one commit, and a line tells you it happened. A contributor gets the same fold: the proposal that lands in review already carries both edits. Only when the two genuinely changed the same lines does Hanji stop, and even then it never dead-ends. It shows you what the other side changed and offers doors, none of which discard your work or theirs: **Keep my version** keeps your wording where you both changed the same lines and folds in the rest of their edit; **Take theirs** loads their page and keeps your draft recoverable; **Propose** sends that same merge to review and leaves the page on theirs. A contributor, or anyone on a suggest mount, sees two doors, because for them Keep mine is the propose door: **Propose my version** and **Take theirs**. The save itself still re-checks the file on disk at the last moment, so nothing is ever overwritten unseen, and this holds on plain folders too, where no git history could bring an overwritten change back.

## New pages

Making a page is the same gesture pointed at a path that does not exist yet. The fastest way is the + that appears at the end of every sidebar row: on a mount it creates at the root, on a folder it creates inside it, and on a page it nests, converting that page into its section's landing with the new page beneath. The title starts empty under an **Untitled** placeholder, and the path below it follows what you type; a page saved with no title is named Untitled. Enter in the title moves on to the body, which says **Start writing** until you do. Document, and press **Create**. That first press is the commit that creates the file; on a mount where you propose, it reads Propose.

<figure><img src="assets/new-page.gif" alt="A new page: a title typed over Untitled, a first line, Update, and the page exists in the tree"><figcaption>A title, a line, Update. The file now exists, and the sidebar already knows.</figcaption></figure>

## Organizing the sheet

The sidebar is not just a map. It is where you arrange the collection.

- **Move**: drag a page or folder onto another folder, or onto a mount's header for its root. A folder brings everything inside it, and the commit behind the drop is a real `git mv`, so history follows the page.
- **Reorder**: drop on the edge of a sibling row, where the insertion line shows. Hanji writes the new arrangement into the pages' `order:` frontmatter, as one commit. This is the *manual* order, and it is the default the sidebar shows.
- **Nest**: drop onto the middle of a page and it becomes a section landing with the dragged page inside, the same conversion the + performs.
- **The rail too**: drag one mount header onto another to reorder the mounts themselves.

Drops apply instantly; git catches up behind. If something blocks a move, the tree snaps back and a toast tells you why. And if you were reading the page you just moved, the address quietly follows it.

### Sorting a section

The curated `order:` is not the only way to read a folder. Open a folder (or a mount) and a small sort control appears on its row: leave it **Manual** to keep your arrangement, or switch that section to **Newest first**, **Oldest first**, or **A–Z** by title. The date it sorts by is the one in the filename when a page has one (a `2026-04-24-…` note sorts by that), and the page's last-commit date otherwise - so a bulk rename that resets git's dates does not scramble the order. The choice is per folder and per person, kept in your browser, so it never changes what anyone else sees or writes anything to the repository. A re-sorted section keeps its control lit so you can tell at a glance. While a section is sorted, drag-to-reorder pauses there: the order you see is not the stored one, so switch back to Manual to curate again.

History, Annotations, Delete and Share sit together in one quiet action group. Edit stays separate as the primary action; all controls align in height and the shortcut follows the theme.

![The document action group](assets/document-page-actions.png)

## Deleting

Next to Edit sits a quiet trash. The first click arms it into an explicit red question, the second deletes: a `git rm` and one commit. Deleting a section landing takes its children with it, the inverse of nesting. Nothing is ever truly gone, though. The repository remembers every sheet, and history can bring one back.

## Activity

In the desktop app, Activity opens in its own workspace view without navigating through Document. It starts with all products; Back returns to the product and page you were using.

Activity starts with a workspace overview: contributions in the last seven days compared with the previous seven, active days, the most active day, product mix and the balance of human, agent and outside contributions. Product bars open that product’s filter. These are recorded contributions, including each credited hand; they do not estimate time saved or productivity. Capped history is labeled as partial.

The first open shows the page shell before it reads history. Data then loads through the authenticated, private `/api/activity` route. A failed or slow request offers Retry and leaves the rest of the app usable. Returning to the page keeps its existing view; Refresh insights asks for current data. Filter links keep their bookmarkable addresses, update in the same document and support browser Back.

Activity is also the workspace's journal: what moved in Document, Plan and Think, and what agents did, by day. Each row reads in one order: the time (or a span, when a run of edits folds into one row), the product in small quiet capitals, who, what, where, and a detail when one matters (where a page moved from, how an issue closed). A page edited thirty times in an hour is one row; a board changed by two people in turn is one row naming both; an agent's session on an issue is one row that names the issue, then the pages and issues it changed, then how long it ran, as in "scribe for ada worked on HNJ-12 Pick the launch date guide/plan · 40 min", and it reads "is working on" while it runs. Every row links into its product: a page, an issue, a board, a session.

![Workspace insights above the journal](assets/activity-insights.png)

![Activity on a narrow screen](assets/activity-insights-mobile.png)

The strip above counts eight weeks of acts by day, humans above the line and agents below it, with each day's split by product in its title. Three filters sit under it, each a link you can bookmark: a product (Document, Plan, Think), a kind of hand (humans, agents, outside), and **Who**, a menu of everyone who moved something in the window. The strip follows the product filter and ignores the others, so the balance of hands stays in view; a caption under it says what it counts. Older takes you back a page at a time, as far as the history goes.

You see only what you may read: a page, an issue or a board outside your grants makes no row, no count in the strip and no name in the menu, and a product you read no mount of has no pill. A commit that also touched something you may not see keeps its verb and loses its message. The "seen up to here" line is a position, moved when you leave the unfiltered journal; nothing is marked read by being seen.

## History

Every page carries its past. Open its history to see who changed it and when, as a list of revisions with a byline, and open any revision to read the page as it was then. Because the store is git, this is not a feature bolted on top. It is the commits, shown well.

<figure><img src="assets/history.gif" alt="Browsing a page's history: the list of revisions with bylines, then reading one as it was"><figcaption>The page's past: every revision, and any of them readable as it was.</figcaption></figure>

Read [[Agents]] next, to let a coding agent read and propose against these same pages.
