<!-- handbook/product/performance.md -->

---
title: Performance
order: 40
description: Paper-thin. The speed and size numbers, measured, and the ones still pending.
---

# Performance

Paper-thin is not only a metaphor about longevity. It is also a claim about weight. A knowledge base you read all day should be quick and light, and most are neither, because every read is a round-trip to someone's cloud and every page ships a small application to your browser.

Hanji is built the other way. Reads come off a local git clone and a small local index, not a network hop. Here are the numbers, measured on the instance we live in daily, with the ones we have not earned yet marked as such. Honesty about limits applies to benchmarks too.

These are recorded measurements of the document/search plane on the stated
corpus, not a benchmark of the complete desktop app, canvas rendering or every
first load. Their setup matters; do not read them as a promise for another machine.

## The agent read path

This is the one that has to be fast, because agents read constantly, measured on the 34,726-page corpus (corpus A). A page fetch and the title tier are measured over 127.0.0.1 against the running instance, five runs each. The four search rows below are p50s from `packages/core/bench/probe.ts`, one timed call per corpus A bench case (42 cases), run in process rather than over the wire.

| Operation | Time | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Fetch a page | ~3 ms | Return a page's Markdown by mount and path |
| Palette, 8 rows | 126.5 ms | Query the FTS5 index across every pages mount you can read |
| Palette, scoped to one mount | 45.1 ms | The same query for a reader who holds part of the tree |
| Results, 20 rows | 107.1 ms | The same query, paged past the palette's eight |
| Results, scoped to one mount | 43.3 ms | The same query for a reader who holds part of the tree |
| Title suggestions as you type | ~11 ms | The two-character prefix the palette fires from |

A page fetch and the title tier stay single-digit to low tens of milliseconds. A full search over this 34,726-page corpus runs about a tenth of a second unscoped and tens of milliseconds for a reader who holds part of the tree; on the 959-page corpus in the "Fifth run, 2026-09-19" sub-section below, every one of these paths stays under 25 ms.

## Indexing at scale

The first sync is the expensive moment: every page is parsed, stored, and
full-text indexed. Measured on a real corpus, on the same machine as above.

| Operation | Time | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| First sync, 34,726 pages | ~4.4 min | Clone-to-searchable, the same pipeline at stress-test size |
| Re-derive an existing index at version 2 | ~3.2 min | The one-time upgrade, run from Settings with progress |

The cost stays near-linear because index writes run in batched transactions
and the full-text rows are addressed by rowid; an earlier build paid a scan
of the whole growing index per page, which turned the 35,000-page sync into
half an hour. Re-syncs only pull what changed in git first, and the indexing
pass yields to the event loop as it runs, so a big sync never freezes the
instance serving it.

A full rebuild of the 34,726-page corpus lands at 866 MB after optimize and
VACUUM, up from 818 MB at version 1, measured on the same corpus before the
format change. The difference is the sections index: five full-text tables
where the previous format carried one, and that is plainly what bought
passage-level landing, jumping to the paragraph a query matched instead of
just the page.

## What the search numbers were measured on

The p50s on this page come from a hand-ranked bench of real queries against
real content, held outside this repository: corpus A is 34,726 pages with 36
targeted judged queries (42 cases total), corpus B is 959 pages with 55
targeted judged queries (82 cases total). Both tables above are corpus A end
to end, so no row compares a small corpus against a large one. Corpus B's
numbers, which pass every budget the spec sets, are in the "Fifth run,
2026-09-19" sub-section below rather than mixed in here. The ranking
constants that decide what ranks first were swept against both sets once and
frozen; see `packages/core/bench/RESULTS.md` for the sweep.

## Weight and dependencies

| Thing | Number |
|---|---|
| Bundled LLM SDKs | 0 |
| AI credits or metering | none, ever |
| Web app runtime dependencies | 24, all ProseMirror, remark-rehype, React, and Next |
| Test cases | 1070 |
| Real Markdown files round-tripped byte-identical | 600+ |

The zero on the first row is the point. Hanji ships no model and meters nothing, so nothing about its cost or its weight grows because your team wrote more this month.

## Weight in the browser

Measured on a clean production build, served and loaded through a real request (the `pnpm smoke` boot test).

| Thing | Number |
|---|---|
| Shared JavaScript, first load | ~103 kB |
| Reading a page, first load | ~108 kB |
| A rendered page, over the wire | ~14 kB of HTML |
| Time to first byte | ~55 ms |

Reading sits just above the shared floor. The editor is a separate chunk that does not load until you press Edit, so the common case, reading, stays paper-thin, and the writing tools arrive only when you reach for them.

## Search, measured 2026-09-18

The search engine was rebuilt from the retrieval layer up. These are the
numbers it ships with, measured against two real corpora on one laptop: a
34,726-page corpus and a 959-page one. The budgets come from the spec, and
not all of them are met yet. They are written down anyway, because a budget
you quietly drop is not a budget.

The dated sections that follow supersede this one: its query timings and its
gate verdicts were all true when measured and have all since changed. Read the
last dated section for where things stand, and this one for where they started.

### Building the index

| Corpus | Pages | Re-derive the whole index | Integrity findings |
|---|---|---|---|
| corpus A | 34,726 | 193 s | 0 |
| corpus B | 959 | 9 s | 0 |

That is a full re-derivation from stored page content, not a git sync, which
is the expensive path an index-format change takes.

| Corpus | index.db before compaction | after optimize and VACUUM | Budget |
|---|---|---|---|
| corpus A | 873,287,680 bytes (873 MB) | 852,533,248 bytes (853 MB) | 1.0 GB |
| corpus B | 82,677,760 bytes (83 MB) | 43,728,896 bytes (44 MB) | none |

Corpus A sits inside the 1.0 GB budget with about 15 percent to spare, and it
carries five full-text tables where the previous index carried one. Corpus B
halves on compaction; corpus A barely moves, because a re-derivation that
large reuses the pages the dropped tables freed instead of growing the file.

### Query latency

p50 and p95 over every judged query in each set, warm index, one process.

| Path | Corpus A p50 | Corpus A p95 | Corpus B p50 | Corpus B p95 | Budget |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Palette, 8 rows | 264.4 ms | 371.9 ms | 18.3 ms | 37.4 ms | 40 ms |
| Palette, scoped to one mount | 64.5 ms | 100.4 ms | 12.0 ms | 26.0 ms | 40 ms |
| Results, 20 rows | 271.0 ms | 385.3 ms | 17.0 ms | 33.7 ms | 80 ms |
| Results, scoped to one mount | 63.7 ms | 101.1 ms | 12.8 ms | 28.6 ms | 80 ms |
| Exact counts | 468.3 ms | 663.6 ms | 18.1 ms | 37.3 ms | 150 ms |
| Exact counts, one term excluded | 560.5 ms | 777.1 ms | 18.2 ms | 37.2 ms | not budgeted |

Corpus B is comfortably inside every budget. Corpus A is over four of the five
budgeted paths, by 1.6x on the scoped palette and by as much as 6.6x on the
unscoped one. The shape of the miss is the useful part: restricting a reader
to one mount makes the same query four times faster, so the cost tracks how
much of the corpus a query can reach and not the permission filter. At 35,000
pages the retrieval pass is still proportional to the number of rows that
match, which is the next thing to fix.

There is a CI tripwire on a generated 5,000-page fixture, budgeted at 25 ms at
p50. Run on its own it holds for a two-word English query (15 to 17 ms) and for
1- and 2-character title prefixes (about 4 ms), and misses on a two-group
Korean query (35 to 38 ms), which fetches roughly twice the rows because the
Korean path adds two more candidate pools. It is not wired into CI yet for that
reason, and because timings taken inside a parallel test suite measure the
suite's other workers as much as the engine.

### Relevance

Scored against judged sets: for each query, the pages a person typing it meant,
best first. MRR is the reciprocal rank of the best target, hit@k the share of
queries with a target in the top k.

| Set | n | MRR | hit@1 | hit@5 | hit@20 | No results |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| corpus A, previous engine | 36 | 0.277 | 22.2% | 33.3% | 47.2% | not recorded |
| corpus A, this engine | 36 | 0.462 | 38.9% | 55.6% | 63.9% | 0.0% |
| corpus B, this engine | 55 | 0.566 | 41.8% | 80.0% | 87.3% | 0.0% |

On the same corpus and the same 36 judged queries, the rebuild moved MRR up 67
percent and nearly doubled hit@1. Latency at p50 went the other way by about
15 percent, from 234.9 ms to 271.0 ms: the engine now reads section text,
scores passages and decides presence in JavaScript, and that is what the
relevance was bought with. Both corpora now return something for every judged
query. The previous engine's zero-result rate was not recorded, so that last
column improves on nothing; it is a floor to hold, not a win to claim.

Counted over every query including the ones with no judged target, which can
never be hit, corpus A reads 0.396 MRR and corpus B 0.379. Those are the
honest denominators for "how often does search help at all"; the table above is
the one that compares to the older measurement.

### Second run, same day: two redundant reads removed

Two numbers were being fetched twice per search. The corpus row counts, which
are the IDF denominators, are now read once per open index instead of twice per
query, and each term's per-table index count is read once per search instead of
twice. Separately, the scorer now reads the per-section term presence that the
earlier phase already decided, instead of deciding it again. None of the three
changes what a search returns; the relevance block below is identical to the one
above, to three decimals, which is how they were checked.

| Path | Corpus A p50 | was | Corpus B p50 | was | Budget |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Palette, 8 rows | 224.6 ms | 264.4 | 17.2 ms | 18.3 | 40 ms |
| Palette, scoped to one mount | **38.5 ms** | 64.5 | 10.7 ms | 12.0 | 40 ms |
| Results, 20 rows | 192.5 ms | 271.0 | 14.0 ms | 17.0 | 80 ms |
| Results, scoped to one mount | 36.8 ms | 63.7 | 10.5 ms | 12.8 | 80 ms |
| Exact counts | 379.5 ms | 468.3 | 14.7 ms | 18.1 | 150 ms |
| Exact counts, one term excluded | 475.1 ms | 560.5 | 15.0 ms | 18.2 | not budgeted |

The scoped palette path moves inside its budget, so corpus A now meets two of
the five, and every path on both corpora is faster. The three still outside are
the unscoped ones, by 5.6x, 2.4x and 2.5x. They are dominated by one index read
whose cost tracks how many rows a query matches rather than how many it returns,
and fixing that is a schema question rather than a tuning one.

Relevance, unchanged by all three:

| Set | n | MRR | hit@1 | hit@5 | hit@20 | No results |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| corpus A | 36 | 0.462 | 38.9% | 55.6% | 63.9% | 0.0% |
| corpus B | 55 | 0.566 | 41.8% | 80.0% | 87.3% | 0.0% |

The CI tripwire on the 5,000-page fixture also improved: the two-word English
query now reads 13.6 ms and the title prefixes 3.7 to 3.9 ms, all inside the
25 ms budget, and the two-group Korean query 27.4 to 28.5 ms, down from 32 to 38
but still over it. The tripwire is still not wired into CI for that one case.

### Third run, same day: the candidate pools stop sorting by date

The two indexes that find Korean and other non-spaced text are candidate
generators: they carry no relevance score, so whatever order their cut takes is
arbitrary. It took the page's edit date, which is the one order that cannot ride
an index, so a common Korean term matched 20,630 sections and all of them were
sorted to return 208. They now take the cut in index order instead, which costs
nothing to produce, and that one statement went from 63.3 ms to 0.6 ms.

| Path | Corpus A p50 | was | and before that | Corpus B p50 | Budget |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Palette, 8 rows | 142.5 ms | 224.6 | 264.4 | 17.1 ms | 40 ms |
| Palette, scoped to one mount | **37.1 ms** | 38.5 | 64.5 | 10.4 ms | 40 ms |
| Results, 20 rows | 116.5 ms | 192.5 | 271.0 | 13.1 ms | 80 ms |
| Results, scoped to one mount | **35.1 ms** | 36.8 | 63.7 | 10.5 ms | 80 ms |
| Exact counts | 316.0 ms | 379.5 | 468.3 | 15.3 ms | 150 ms |
| Exact counts, one term excluded | 408.9 ms | 475.1 | 560.5 | 14.8 ms | not budgeted |

Across the three runs the palette path is 46 percent faster, the results path 57
percent, and the exact counts 33 percent, on the large corpus. Corpus B passes
every budget. Corpus A still misses the three unscoped paths, now by 3.6x, 1.5x
and 2.1x rather than 6.6x, 3.4x and 3.1x.

Relevance, unchanged again:

| Set | n | MRR | hit@1 | hit@5 | hit@20 | No results |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| corpus A | 36 | 0.462 | 38.9% | 55.6% | 63.9% | 0.0% |
| corpus B | 55 | 0.566 | 41.8% | 80.0% | 87.3% | 0.0% |

Worth one honest note: identical scores do not mean identical results. The new
cut changes which candidates survive on 13 of the 42 judged queries, 50 pages in
all. Every one of them was a page no judge had named, so no target moved, which
is the evidence that the old order was not buying relevance. It is not evidence
that the cut never matters.

The latency tripwire now passes, and it is wired into a gate rather than into
CI: `pnpm test:gates` runs the suite and then the tripwire. There is no CI
workflow in this repository at all, so nothing runs either of them on a push;
the gate is what a person or an agent runs before a commit. The tripwire lives
in its own file and runs alone, with file parallelism off, as `pnpm --filter
@hanji/core test:latency`; it is kept out of the default test run on purpose,
because a timing assertion sharing a machine with the rest of the suite
measures the suite. On the
5,000-page fixture, three runs: a two-word query 13.7 to 14.3 ms unscoped and
12.5 to 13.0 scoped, a two-group Korean query 23.9 to 24.7 ms, and 1- and
2-character title prefixes 3.7 ms. Every budget here follows one rule: about
1.5x the case's own isolated p50, rounded up to the next 5 ms. The title
prefixes keep the 25 ms that gives them, clearing it by about seven times
over. The two-word cases and the Korean case now sit at 30 ms and 40 ms
instead, once the fourth run's constant-depth pooling raised their own
measurements to 19.9 ms and 26.8 ms: at the old 25 ms and 35 ms they would
clear by only a few percent, and a tripwire with that little headroom flakes
on a busy machine long before it catches a real regression. What the Korean
budget defends against is a regression of 40 percent or more on that shape.

### Fourth run, 2026-09-18: one candidate set per query

The pool depth was the offset plus the page size, so page 2 pooled deeper than
page 1 and could retrieve a candidate ranking above a row page 1 had already
served. Walking a 700-page fixture twenty rows at a time served 96 pages twice
and never reached 306 of the 700. Any request that pages, or asks for more rows
than the palette's eight, now pools at the cap, so every page of one query is a
slice of one candidate set. The palette keeps the shallow pool: it never pages,
and its budget is the tight one.

That is retrieval depth bought with time. The row that says so is the same run
with the old depth, measured minutes apart on the same machine, because the
numbers below are about 10 percent slower than the third run's across the board
including on the palette, which this change cannot touch.

| Path | Corpus A p50 | same run, old depth | Corpus B p50 | same run, old depth | Budget |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Palette, 8 rows | 159.3 ms | 149.5 | 15.4 ms | 16.2 | 40 ms |
| Palette, scoped to one mount | 56.9 ms | 51.6 | 9.5 ms | 9.9 | 40 ms |
| Results, 20 rows | 136.6 ms | 126.7 | 22.5 ms | 12.1 | 80 ms |
| Results, scoped to one mount | 54.5 ms | 50.5 | 15.1 ms | 9.4 | 80 ms |
| Exact counts | 367.5 ms | 342.9 | 24.8 ms | 14.3 | 150 ms |

On corpus B the cost is plain: the results path went from 12.1 ms to 22.5 ms and
the exact counts from 14.3 to 24.8, because on a 959-page corpus a 500-row pool
is a large share of everything there is to fetch. On corpus A the results path
moved 7.8 percent, which is what the palette moved in the same pair of runs
without being touched, so at that size the change is at the machine's noise
floor: the pool is bounded by how many rows match, not by the cap. Corpus B
stays inside every budget. Corpus A misses four this time rather than three: the
three unscoped paths, and the scoped palette, which read 37.1 ms in the third run
and reads 51.6 ms in this run's old-depth control as well, so what moved it is
the machine and not the change.

Relevance did NOT stay identical this time, and that is the point of the change:

| Set | n | MRR | hit@1 | hit@5 | hit@20 | No results |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| corpus A | 36 | **0.472** | 38.9% | **58.3%** | **69.4%** | 0.0% |
| corpus B | 55 | 0.566 | 41.8% | 80.0% | 87.3% | 0.0% |

Corpus A read 0.462 MRR, 55.6 percent hit@5 and 63.9 percent hit@20 for three
runs; what moved them is judged targets the shallow pool cut before anything
could rank them. Over every query including the untargeted ones, corpus A reads
0.405 against 0.396 and corpus B 0.380 against 0.379. Corpus B's judged block is
identical to three decimals, which is the check the previous three runs were held
to: its 959 pages were almost always inside the shallow pool already. The
old-depth control run reproduced all six of the previous numbers exactly, which
is how this change was attributed rather than assumed.

The latency tripwire on the 5,000-page fixture still passes every case at its
budget. The same constant paging depth that moved the benchmark table above
also moved the tripwire's own two-word gate cases, from about 13 ms to about
20 ms.

### Fifth run, 2026-09-19: rebuild and exact-pass numbers re-taken

A `hanji rebuild` over the same 34,726-page corpus, git tree included, took
263 s: about 70 s longer than the 193 s `reindexAll` measured earlier for the
same page count, because `rebuild` re-reads and re-parses every file from the
mounted tree first and `reindexAll` only re-derives the index from content
already stored in `pages`.

Corpus A's palette, results path and exact pass, against the spec's budgets:

| Path | Corpus A p50 | Budget | Meets it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Palette, 8 rows | 126.5 ms | 40 ms | no |
| Palette, scoped to one mount | 45.1 ms | 40 ms | no |
| Results, 20 rows | 107.1 ms | 80 ms | no |
| Results, scoped to one mount | 43.3 ms | 80 ms | yes |
| Exact counts | 285.2 ms | 150 ms | no |

Corpus B, 959 pages, every path:

| Path | Corpus B p50 | Budget | Meets it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Palette, 8 rows | 14.9 ms | 40 ms | yes |
| Palette, scoped to one mount | 8.7 ms | 40 ms | yes |
| Results, 20 rows | 20.9 ms | 80 ms | yes |
| Results, scoped to one mount | 15.1 ms | 80 ms | yes |
| Exact counts | 22.2 ms | 150 ms | yes |

Corpus B meets every budget the spec sets. Corpus A meets one of the five
(the scoped results path); the other four miss by 3.2x, 1.1x, 1.3x and 1.9x
(palette, scoped palette, results, the exact pass).

The exact pass on corpus A is the widest miss here, at roughly 1.9x its
150 ms budget. There is no "500+" fallback on the results page for this: the
exact pass always runs inline, and the count line reads "N results, M match
every term" when the two differ, or a plain "N results" when they agree. A
list-first variant, rendering the list before the counts resolve, is the
recorded post-launch option for hiding that latency. The exact pass's
transient heap at 35,000 pages is the other recorded residual: the unbounded
pass holds
every matching row to compute `total` and `totalAny`, and that has not been
profiled or bounded yet.

See `packages/core/bench/RESULTS.md` for the ranking sweep these numbers were
measured against. That sweep moved corpus A from 0.472 to 0.490 MRR and
corpus B from 0.566 to 0.579.

### Acceptance checks

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| A large attachment manifest does not move a title-exact match | pass |
| A term matching mid-word ranks below one matching at a word start | pass, over the returned page of 20 |
| A glued mixed-script term does not widen to pages holding its halves apart | pass |

The index itself is worth one honest note. It is a cache. Whatever it costs in space, you can delete it and rebuild it from git, because the repository is the only thing that has to be trusted. Read [[Byte-fidelity]] for the engine underneath, and [[Why Hanji is different]] for why none of this is bundled.

<!-- handbook/product/permissions.md -->

---
title: Permissions
order: 20
description: The two-plane model, and exactly what it enforces today.
---

# Permissions

Permissions are where most knowledge tools get honest too late. Hanji tries to get honest early, which means telling you plainly what the lock does today and what it does not do yet.

## The model

Two planes. One is an open human front, where a team reads and writes in the clear. The other is the set of sensitive areas that must stay closed, the meeting notes and the decisions and anything you would not tack to a shared wall. The whole design rests on one rule: **every surface honors the same check**. Search, wikilinks, page reads, and the agent tools all ask the same question before they show you anything, so there is no back door where a locked title slips out through search, or a link resolves to a page you were never allowed to open.

That is not a claim to make lightly, so here is how it actually works.

## One read path

Every read Hanji serves runs through a single module. The scope check, which mounts may this reader see, is compiled in exactly one place and nowhere else. Search filters to your readable mounts before it runs. A page read returns nothing for a mount you cannot see. Wikilink resolution uses the same filter. This is the boring, load-bearing part. There is one door, and it is the same door for people and for agents.

A locked page and a page that does not exist look identical to a reader who lacks access. Both come back as not found. You cannot probe the shape of what you are not allowed to see.

## Scopes today

Access is granted per mount, in three levels.

| Scope | The reader can | The reader cannot |
|---|---|---|
| none | see nothing of the mount, not even that it exists | read, search, or link into it |
| `read` | read, search, and follow links inside the mount | write, or propose changes |
| `read+propose` | everything `read` can, plus propose changes as a branch or PR | merge, or write directly |
| `read+write` | everything `read+propose` can, plus commit to base from the front and upload images | merge, or restructure the tree |

`read+write` is for people only: a token never holds it.

The owner sees every mount. An agent gets a bearer token whose scopes take the same shape as a person's grants - on a pages mount, a whole mount, a folder, or exactly one page - so an agent that helps with the engineering docs never sees the folder of sensitive notes, even when both live in the same repository. See [[Agents]] for how that works in practice. The agents Hanji Plan runs hold one such token each, named `agent-<handle>`, which the tracker and its session host read by name in process, with no bearer in hand. The token scopes Hanji's own tools, prompts and briefs; a Plan session also runs on the owner's machine, where the operating-system user is the boundary (see [[Agents]]).

## Visibility belongs to the content

The model reads the way Notion and Confluence taught everyone to think. Content carries a general access level - **Everyone can read**, **Everyone can suggest**, or **Restricted** - set on a mount, a folder, or a single page (on a pages mount; see Grants on a tracker and on boards below), flowing down to everything beneath (a tracker takes Everyone can read or Restricted; read plus suggest equals read there). Open content is simply open: no per-person bookkeeping. Restricted content is dark by default, and the deepest rule covering a page wins, so one restricted folder inside an open mount goes dark for everyone.

People are the exceptions. A person granted a path - on a pages mount, a mount, a folder, or exactly one page - punches through a restriction at or below their grant. That is the 1:1 note: a restricted folder, two names, and nobody else sees it in the tree, in search, or through a wikilink. A locked page still looks identical to a page that does not exist.

Sharing lives where the content lives (in team mode - solo keeps this chrome hidden until you switch, in Settings): a **Share** control on every page, and on every mount and folder in the sidebar, showing the general access (and where it is inherited from), the people with specific access and through which grant, and a one-line way to add someone with read, suggest, or edit. Settings keeps the overview: a Mount access tab for general access per mount, and a People tab for everyone's grants in one place. Revoking takes effect on the person's next request. The rule and grant tables are the implementation; the page is the interface.

<figure><img src="assets/share-popover.png" alt="The Share popover on a mount: general access set to Everyone can read, and one person's grant listed beneath" class="w-75"><figcaption>Share, where the content lives: the general rule on top, the exceptions by name.</figcaption></figure>

One deliberate exception: **agents never inherit "everyone"**. A token sees exactly the scopes it was minted with, whatever the content rules say - opening a mount to your team never opens it to a bot.

## People, same scopes

The same levels apply to humans. The owner adds a person in Settings with a name, a password, and per-mount scopes: `read` makes a **viewer**, `read+propose` makes a **contributor** whose Update reads Propose and lands in the owner's review card, and `read+write` makes an **editor** whose Update commits to base, the way the owner's does. Nobody but the owner restructures the tree, reviews proposals, or sees settings. In user terms: viewers read, contributors suggest, editors write, the owner decides. One read path, one review ceremony, whatever species the writer is.

## Grants on a tracker and on boards

A work mount, which holds a tracker, and a think mount, which holds boards, take the same three levels, named for what each allows there:

| Mount | `read` | `read+propose` | `read+write` |
|---|---|---|---|
| pages | viewer: reads and searches | contributor: proposes changes | editor: commits from the front |
| work | viewer: sees the tracker | the same as `read` | editor: changes issues |
| think | viewer: sees the boards | commenter: comments and reacts | editor: edits the boards |

Settings offers Viewer and Editor on a work mount, and Viewer, Commenter and Editor on a think mount, and tags those mounts as tracker and boards. A grant or a general-access rule on a work mount covers the whole mount, so every reader of the tracker sees the same issues; on a think mount it covers the mount, a folder of boards or one board, at any depth. Hanji Plan honors these grants on a tailnet. View (`read`) opens the tracker; without it, every Plan address answers 404, the same for an issue that exists and one that does not. Edit (`read+write`) with an entry under `people:` in the tracker file lets a person change issues and file an issue from a page in Document or from a sticky in Think, as themselves. The owner can do both without a `people:` entry. A person who may write a mount of pages, or propose on one, can write up a board section or a selection as a page there from Think, as themselves; a proposal lands in Document's review, on a local mount as a branch of the folder's own repository. Undo deletes only the page that press wrote, within the notice's ten seconds; deleting any other page stays in Document. Actions that let an agent run code on the owner's machine stay with the owner, whatever the grant. Hanji Think honors these grants too: a Viewer opens a board, a Commenter comments, reacts and votes in an open voting session, an Editor edits it and facilitates timers and voting; without a grant on a board, every Think address for it answers 404, the same as for a board that does not exist. On a tailnet, Document, Plan and Think sign a request in by its tailnet login only when its `Host` is this machine's loopback address or the host of one of the product addresses (`HANJI_KB_URL`, `HANJI_TRACKER_URL`, `HANJI_THINK_URL`), so a web page open on the same machine cannot sign itself in. See [[On your tailnet]].

Cited by follows the work mount's grants: a page lists an issue only for a reader who can read the tracker's mount.

## What is honest about it

One residual is worth naming. Ranking statistics are counted under your own scope, so indexing a page you cannot read no longer moves the order or the scores you see. What is still global is the relevance figure SQLite's FTS5 computes inside the candidate pool and the page base score: its inverse document frequency counts the whole index. A reader who shapes queries and watches fine-grained order changes over time could infer roughly how often a term occurs in content outside their scope. Closing it means computing the base score in code over the text we already fetch, with scoped frequencies, and keeping FTS5's figure only to cut the candidate pool. That is planned, not done.

The unit of permission on a pages mount is now the path, down to one file (the section above covers the other kinds), for people and agent tokens alike, and it holds on the same single read path as everything else. What remains honest to say: product privacy is not storage privacy - the bytes are plaintext in a git repo, so the instance owner and the git host can always read them. A 1:1 note is hidden from every other principal; hiding it from the owner would take cryptography, which permissions do not provide. The two-plane model is real and enforced on one honest read path, and [[Where we are]] tracks the rest without rounding up.

---

<!-- handbook/product/two-faces.md -->

---
title: The two faces
order: 10
description: One knowledge base, a human face and an agent face, over the same git.
---

# The two faces

Most tools are built for one reader and then bolt on the other. A wiki built for people adds an AI chat box. An agent tool built for machines adds a rough editor and hopes the humans cope. Hanji starts from the fact that both read the same knowledge, and gives each the surface it actually wants, over the same git underneath.

## The human face

A person should never have to think about git to write down what they know.

So the front hides it completely. You open a page and it reads like a good magazine, cool neutral paper and a serif set for long reading. You click Edit, the page becomes editable in place, you change what you came to change, and you press Update. Behind that one button, Hanji writes a single commit with a clean message and a full history. No staging, no branch names, no merge dialog. And if you change nothing, nothing is committed, because there was nothing to record.

Under the calm surface is a real editor. Tables with the controls you expect, task lists you can check off, a slash menu to insert, images that upload into the repo itself, and embeds for the tools you already use. It stays out of your way, and it never rewrites a line you did not touch. See [[Byte-fidelity]] for why that last part matters more than it sounds.

## The agent face

An agent should not have to pretend to be a browser to read your docs.

Agents already live in git, so the first face for them is git itself. They clone, they read files, they search, all at local speed, with no API throttle and no hosted round-trip. Where a live surface helps, a small MCP server gives them scoped search and reading through the same permission check a person gets. And when an agent wants to contribute, it does not reach into a page and overwrite it. It proposes a change as a branch, and where GitHub is connected, as a pull request. A person reviews it in the front and merges. The agent suggests, you decide, and your history never fills up with edits nobody approved.

## The same git underneath

The point of two faces is that there is one thing behind them. A person edits a page and an agent sees the new bytes on its next read. An agent proposes a branch and a person reviews it on the same warm page they read everything else on. Nobody is working on a copy. It is one knowledge base, and it was your git the whole time.

Read [[What Hanji is]] for the overview, and [[Using Hanji]] when you want to actually drive it.

---

title: Quick start
order: 5
description: From the invited desktop preview to your first canvas, issue or page.
---

# Quick start

The quickest path is the invited Mac desktop preview. [Request access](https://hanji.ink/start/)
if you do not have a copy. Public binary downloads are not available yet, and
source access is shared separately with preview participants.

## With the desktop preview

1. Move Hanji.app to Applications and open it.
2. Choose Create your workspace, give it a name, and select Think, Plan and/or Document.
3. Choose Start fresh to let Hanji prepare folders, or bring existing content.
4. Choose an owner password, review, and create the workspace.

[[Desktop workspace]] explains each stage, recovery, and the workspace shell.

![The workspace setup](assets/onboarding-workspace.png)

## Make the first thing

- **Think:** create a canvas, add a sticky, and connect it to another idea.
- **Plan:** create an issue; a clear title is enough to start.
- **Document:** open the welcome page, edit a sentence and save it.

Your files stay local. The conductor is optional: configure your own agent later
through Settings. See [[The conductor]] for provider setup, context and approval.

## With an existing source checkout

Development dependencies and a working Git installation are required. The
SQLite native module must match the Node runtime used to run the checkout.
Follow that checkout’s prerequisites, then:

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm dev:web   # → http://localhost:4100
```

The first visit uses the same guided setup. [[Install Hanji]] covers explicit
configuration for a source checkout or server. These commands assume access to
the source; they are not a public download link.

## Where next

[[Think canvas]], [[Objectives and key results]], [[Reading and writing]] and
[[Workspace insights]] cover the daily tools. [[Mounts]] adds existing content,
and [[On your tailnet]] shares it with people you authorize.

<!-- handbook/status.md -->

---
title: Where we are
order: 120
description: What is shipped, what is next, and what we are still exploring.
---

# Where we are now

Hanji is a research lab exploring how people interact with agents. The current workspace is a working result of that research, shaped by an individual need and continued iteration. [[Mission and vision]] explains the purpose; this page describes what can be used today and what is still being explored.

## Public handbook

The public handbook has a product-oriented start page, grouped navigation, local page-title search and section links with an on-page outline. A compact header keeps site identity and theme controls together. Previous/next links follow the published guide order; Markdown sources remain available. Reading, section links and collapsible navigation work without JavaScript. Search is a client-side filter of exported public navigation, not a search into the live or private workspace.

## Current product

Hanji is an invited Mac desktop preview with three connected surfaces:

- **Think**: live canvases for notes, diagrams, tables and shared workshops. Selected notes can become issues or a written page.
- **Plan**: file-backed issues, projects, dependencies, objectives and key results, with list, board and canvas views.
- **Document**: Markdown reading and editing, scoped search, comments, history, proposals and selective publishing.

The conductor carries a standing agent conversation across the workspace. Agent use is optional and requires your own supported provider setup. Workspace insights show recorded activity across products.

[[What Hanji is]] explains the whole workspace. [[From idea to action]] follows a fictional decision across the three surfaces; [[Using Hanji]] maps the detailed guides. [[Mission and vision]] distinguishes our larger ambition from the preview available today. The [[Changelog]] records individual interface changes.

## Availability and limits

The handbook is public; the app is shared by invitation. There is no unrestricted public binary download or hosted workspace service. The preview runs on your machine or infrastructure you operate. Direct repository access is outside Hanji's permission boundary, and storage and permission models differ by surface. Back up durable configuration and journals as well as repositories.

The public site and handbook publish separately. Product figures use fictional workspaces rendered by the real application; illustrative workflows are not customer results.

## Implemented in the source and desktop preview

- [x] Simplified shared chrome: one search and shortcut entry per view, border-light list/board/objective layouts, and spacing-led drawer and conversation sections.

- [x] Refined bottom ask composer and issue drawer: an integrated workspace thread without page navigation, a configurable conductor shape, segmented agent selection, compact metadata, balanced comments, and consistent sub-issue status indicators. Canvas trace controls sit at the top; the chat shares the zoom-control baseline.

- [x] Hanji Plan (early) with drawer editing, searchable property menus, comment submission feedback, and collapsible history: sortable list columns, board, and canvas, visible saved-view navigation with consistent icons and a searchable persistent icon picker and inline view renaming, compact drawer controls, nearly opaque canvas cards with relationship highlights and semantic zoom with automatic fixed-footprint detail and sharp settled zoom and discreet status silhouettes, balanced board/canvas card layouts and aligned blocking icons, compact group widths, draggable sections with remembered browser-local positions and reset, editable project frames with creation and idea capture plus visible-card bulk edits, direct curved dependencies beneath cards with persistent endpoint markers with consistent drag/rest and bundle routing, inspectable outside blockers, and drawer-aware framing, view context and work counts, issue pages with a return path, and a command menu; optional dependency lanes, direct/full-chain tracing, pin/fit controls, outside-view prerequisite cards, and cycle handling; unified collapsible navigation with compact reversible slide-and-fade motion and view controls, a cool neutral light/dark palette with neutral primary buttons and send actions, and the workspace's own accent on its cool neutral paper, with the workspace accent for in-progress status and fixed colors for other semantic statuses and OKR health and tested text contrast, an integrated canvas arrangement switch and compact docked trace feedback with stable selection ownership and reversible entry/exit motion, and a shortcut reference with field and drawer navigation commands

- [x] Byte-fidelity Markdown engine, guarded by a corpus gate
- [x] Git-backed mounts, sync, and a rebuildable index
- [x] The human front: reading, in-place WYSIWYG editing, history, nested navigation
- [x] The agent surface: MCP scoped read tools and propose-as-branch (a pull request where GitHub is connected)
- [x] Per-mount permissions on a single read path
- [x] The agent git flow, end to end: an agent proposes, you review the diff in the front, and merge (see [[Proposals]])
- [x] Proposals on local mounts: a proposal is a branch of the folder's own repository, reviewed and merged in the same front; proposing and rejecting never touch your checked-out branch or edits; Merge fast-forwards the base in your folder only when it has no uncommitted edits to tracked files, and moves the base's ref alone when the base is checked out nowhere (see [[Proposals]])
- [x] Search worth the name: passage-level retrieval with a workspace-wide title tier, Hangul bigrams and alias classes, under a `⌘K` palette and a results page with exact counts, mount chips and a result that lands you on the passage
- [x] The agent retrieval contract: a search envelope with matched and missing terms, section anchors on `hanji_get_page`, a cursor on `hanji_list_pages`, a capped `hanji_changes`, and `hanji_links` over the page graph
- [x] The sidebar as an organizer: quick-create, drag to move, reorder, nest, and delete, all real git behind an instant UI
- [x] Per-section sorting: a folder or mount sorts its own children by date (newest or oldest, from the filename or the commit) or A-Z - a personal, per-section choice kept in the browser
- [x] Every page's paper trail: a byline of who began it and who last changed it, read from git history, shown on the page and powering the recency sort
- [x] A workspace made yours: name, logo, OKLCH theming with secured contrast, fonts, and a phone-ready shell
- [x] Proposal from the human front: on a suggest-only mount, Update becomes Propose, landing in the same review card
- [x] Several human principals: viewers, contributors, and editors with per-mount scopes, added by the owner in Settings; editors commit to base, contributors propose
- [x] The lock, down to a single page: path grants (on a pages mount: mount, folder, or one file) and a Share button on the page itself
- [x] Content-first visibility: general access inherited downward, restrictions that go dark, people as the exceptions
- [x] Mount kinds and references: Document keeps to pages mounts, a tracker registers as a work mount, and `[[HNJ-12]]` and Cited by follow each reader's grants (see [[Links and references]])
- [x] Tailscale mode: run on a tailnet and the network signs people in, no password, grants untouched (see [[On your tailnet]])
- [x] Path grants for agent tokens: on a pages mount a token holds a mount, a folder, or one page - the same mechanism people have
- [x] `hanji export`: the everyone-visible content mirrored as `llms.txt` plus per-page Markdown, for the agents that read the open web
- [x] Changes arrive on their own: a signed push-to-sync webhook, and an opt-in poll loop for tailnets and local mounts
- [x] A first run without a terminal: four named setup stages, automatic fresh folders, optional imports, an owner password and a final review, then signed-in access
- [x] The publishing plane: `hanji export` renders a browsable static site - the hanji look, no JavaScript - beside the Markdown mirror. This handbook is published with it.
- [x] Fresh by the time you look: sync-on-focus, a byline freshness line, early conflict warning, a content-compare save guard, and agents that sync local mounts before every read
- [x] The freshness note carries a destination: it names the page that moved and links to it, or points at Activity when several did; a change that moved no page refreshes without a note
- [x] Images count as freshness too: a per-mount asset fingerprint makes a replaced picture a change the screen hears about, and stamps the image URLs so the browser cannot answer from its cache
- [x] The Activity page: the workspace's journal of what moved in Document, Plan and Think and what agents did, by day, straight from the history, plus a local mount's edits not yet committed, with honest actor labels and a "seen up to here" line
- [x] The activity strip: eight weeks of days above the journal, human hands above the line, agents below, with filters by product, hand and kind of hand as links
- [x] A concurrent edit arrives early: while the editor sits idle, a cleanly folding change is merged into the open buffer and the caret is put back, instead of waiting at the save
- [x] `hanji digest`: the day's changes and the waiting queue written into the workspace as a page - the artifact is the notification, cron is the only scheduler
- [x] The agent briefing channel: `hanji_changes` / `GET /changes` for "what moved since I last read", plus an Atom feed of the same, token-scoped like every read
- [x] Open Knowledge Format interop: any OKF bundle mounts as-is, and `hanji export --okf` emits a conformant one - typed concept docs, reserved index files, an `okf_version` root
- [x] One sticky chrome bar for reading and editing, and edit mode that swaps in place - same scroll position, same header, only the buttons and the toolbar change
- [x] A selection that stays selected: Copy (as Markdown *and* as rich text) and Comment offered on a bar, rather than the comment box taking the selection
- [x] Highlights in four curated colours, portable `==x==` for the default and `<mark class="hl-...">` for a chosen one (see [[Reading and writing]])
- [x] Page comments: a thread at the foot of every page, and anchored comments on an exact word or sentence, highlighted in the prose for every reader and preserved under "On an earlier version" when the text beneath them changes (see [[Comments]])
- [x] Presence on the page: who else is editing, named beside the byline and inside the editor, and a page that checks itself every few seconds while you look, so a conflict folds at save instead of surprising you

Reading and writing both feel like paper. That was the first thing that had to be true. See [[Features]] for the full list, and [[Changelog]] for what shipped when.

## Plan in the current preview

Hanji Plan's conversations are reworked: a quiet conductor chosen on Plan's Agents page, one conversation per person over the workspace's sessions database, one panel across the three products, one composer everywhere, honest session states. A cleanup pass then made Plan faster, put its styles on one layered design system, and brought it to WCAG 2.2 AA. All of it is local for review; live Claude and GPT sessions have not been exercised by these checks. See [[Features]] for the details.

On a tailnet, Plan now signs teammates in: view on the tracker's work mount opens it, edit with a `people:` entry lets them edit as themselves, and actions that run an agent stay with the owner. See [[On your tailnet]]. In Document, **Issue** on the selection bar files a selected sentence as a Plan issue that cites the page and its heading (see [[Comments]]); in Think, **Create issue** files stickies as issues that cite the board (see [[Think canvas]]), and an issue's page shows where it came from under **From**. In Think, **Write up** turns a section or a selection into a Document page, or a proposal, that names the board it came from. Agents in Plan hold their own Document identity, a token named `agent-<handle>`: they read the knowledge base as it, a Claude session proposes through it, and a project's **Docs**, **Draft a doc** and **Draft a status** live on its group in a view's canvas. A workspace can hold several trackers, each with its own prefix and grants, and Plan, Document and Think reach them all (see [[Mounts]]). A harmony pass then put the three products on one neutral palette (Plan's), took the marks out of their chrome, gave them one product switcher, moved Settings out of Document's shell into a workspace page of its own (with a Document tab for what is Document's), quieted the conductor's dock, and made Think's board list a board of cards with a New board dialog. A second pass put Activity beside Settings as a workspace page, harmonized the search field, softened the primary button to a tint of the accent, redrew Think's islands and moved a selection's actions into one bar above the tools, and gave each board card a preview of its objects. A third pass names the product in each shell, gives the workspace pages a Back control, and puts Think's boards in folders with a sidebar and Recent as the default list.

## Next, in build

A proposed Comments/Actions split is under design review: discussion and mentions should be distinct from explicitly requested execution. The current comment-to-session routing remains in place until that behavior is resolved.

The agent git flow shipped; what remains of the real test is a team living on it daily.

- [ ] **A proper team on a shared instance** - people and agents writing side by side, the proof no more code can produce

## Later, the paid seam

Everything an administrator needs to trust Hanji with a whole organization. This is where the revenue is, and it is deliberately not where the writing is.

| Area | What it adds |
|---|---|
| Hosted sync | A managed instance, for teams who would rather not run their own |
| Single sign-on | Log in with your identity provider |
| Audit | Who read and wrote what, and when, read straight from the git history |
| Hardening | The operational harnesses that keep an organization-size instance honest at scale |

## Exploring, not promised

Ideas we like and have not committed to.

- Production real-time collaboration and deployment: Whiteboard has an early single-server operation-sharing prototype with Git checkpoints, with character-level editing, but not a shipped multi-server service
- Serving a folder as an installable agent skill
- A desktop shell around the web plane, once it can be distributed properly

Read [[Mission and vision]] for the why behind the order.

Canvas relationships use direct Bézier curves beneath cards, best-facing edge anchors, and persistent dot/arrow endpoint markers.

Canvas curves favor the exterior of their project frames, scoring routes by card overlap and time spent inside frames. Direct under-card curves remain a fallback; moved frames update this preference during dragging.

<!-- handbook/story/brand/index.md -->

---
title: The brand
order: 70
description: A thin surface between people and agents: Hanji's identity, look and voice.
---

# The brand

Hanji is a research lab for human–agent interaction. Its central idea is a thin surface between people and agents, bringing enough clarity for people to understand, question and direct the work.

The lab grew from an individual need, through countless iterations. It now shares results publicly and as open source while continuing to explore. The brand should carry that curiosity and care, alongside the practical quality of working tools.

- [[The name]] gives us the paper metaphor: one material, many forms of interaction.
- [[The visual language]] gives the work a calm, readable surface, with editorial typography, restrained color and the ㅎ mark.
- [[Voice]] explains how to write about the research plainly and distinguish working capabilities from ambitions.

## The lab and its products

Lead with the research question and its purpose: clearer interaction and sound human judgment. Then show the workspace as a current expression of that research. Think, Plan and Document deserve clear product explanations, without making their present arrangement the definition of Hanji.

Open formats and ownership support the work. They should be explained as product principles and capabilities. The mission is better interaction with our virtual companions and colleagues.

## The posture

Thoughtful, practical and open to change. Show the actual work and explain what it helps someone understand. Describe where an idea came from, what the current tool does and what remains uncertain. Sharing a result is an invitation to use it and learn from it together.

The visual craft should support clarity. A logo treatment or a setting can be considered carefully without becoming the reason the product exists.

---

<!-- handbook/story/brand/visual-language.md -->

---
title: The visual language
order: 10
description: Cool neutral paper, an editorial serif, celadon, and a mark cut back to its bones.
---

# The visual language

The visual language serves a thin surface between people and agents. Calm paper, readable typography and restrained controls help people understand the work and exercise judgment. Here is how that becomes visible.

## Calm neutral paper

The shared background is a restrained cool off-white (`#f5f6f8`), with near-white sheets (`#fcfcfd`) and slightly deeper navigation (`#eceef1`). Blue-gray ink and borders preserve distinction without a yellow cast. Dark mode carries the same quiet slate undertone. Document, Plan, Think and the desktop shell use this neutral family; workspace accents and content colors keep their identity.

## An editorial serif

The reading type is **Newsreader**, a serif drawn for long-form reading, set large with a generous line-height and a comfortable measure. A knowledge base is a place you read, sometimes for a long time, and it should carry the calm of a good magazine rather than the density of a dashboard. The interface itself steps back into a quiet sans, so the writing stays the loudest thing on the page.

## 비색, the secret color

The accent is a workspace's own choice, and its default is the ink itself, near black, so a fresh workspace is paper and ink and nothing else; a link reads as a link by its underline, a current item by its weight and its fill. **Celadon (비색, bisaek)**, the blue-green glaze of Goryeo celadon that Korean potters a thousand years ago called *the secret color*, stays the color of the product's own story and marketing: calm, unmistakably Korean, almost never seen in software, and tied to a tradition of objects made by hand and meant to endure, which is the same claim hanji makes about paper. A workspace that wants it picks it in Settings.

## The mark

<figure>
<img src="assets/hanji-mark.svg" alt="The Hanji mark, a hieut reduced to a stroke, a bar, and a ring" class="w-25">
<figcaption>ㅎ or hieut from the Korean alphabet (한글)</figcaption>
</figure>

The logo is **ㅎ (hieut)**, the first consonant of 한 in 한지 and Hanji, cut back to its bones: a short top stroke, a horizontal bar, and a ring. The letter was already almost a mark, and we only had to clear away what it did not need. The three parts sit exactly where the letter puts them, so it reads as ㅎ to anyone who knows the alphabet and as a calm, balanced glyph to anyone who does not.

The mark keeps its own deep charcoal whatever accent the workspace chose. The accent belongs to the writing surface, and the mark is the object that sits on the surface, so it holds its own weight, the way a seal pressed into paper is darker than the ink of the page. It is the single, deliberate exception to the color rule.

## Restraint as the style

There is no chrome for its own sake, no gradient, no theatre of shadows. The craft lives in the spacing, the type, and one considered color. Elegance here is a matter of what we left out. Read [[Voice]] for how the same restraint shapes the words.

---

<!-- handbook/story/brand/voice.md -->

---
title: Voice
order: 20
description: "How Hanji speaks: plainly, with an edge, and honest about its limits."
---

# Voice

Hanji's visual language is restraint, and its voice is the same restraint carried into words. Here is how it speaks, and why.

## Plain

We say the thing. No jargon standing in for a plain word, no sentence that could have come from any product on any landing page. If a claim can be made in a shorter word, it is. The reader is a peer, a working engineer or designer who can smell marketing from a mile off, and they get talked to like one.

## With an edge

Plain does not mean bland. Hanji has a point of view: clarity matters when people work with agents, and an interface should support human judgment. Speak from the practical experience of building and using the tools. Give the reader a clear observation, a working example or an honest question.

Describe Hanji as a research lab and the products as current expressions of that research. Explain open formats and ownership where they matter to a workflow. Keep the lab's purpose centered on the interaction between people and agents.

## Honest about limits

This is the load-bearing one. When a feature is not built, we say so. When product privacy is real but storage privacy is not - the bytes stay plaintext in your git, readable by whoever holds the repository - the page says exactly that. A benchmark we have not run honestly is marked as not run, not rounded up. It is the [[Principles]] page applied to the writing: a promise we cannot keep is worse than no promise, so we do not make it.

## In practice

A page reads like a person wrote it, because one did. Sentences vary. Some run long and accumulating, some are three words. There is a wink now and then, and a number wherever a claim can carry one. What there never is: a summary that restates what you just read, or a conclusion that adds nothing. When the point is made, the page stops.

Read [[The visual language]] for the same restraint in pixels.

<!-- handbook/story/index.md -->

---
title: The story
order: 60
description: How a personal need became a research lab for human–agent interaction.
---

# The story

*A thin surface between people and agents.*

Hanji began with an individual need: to work better with agents. As they became more capable, understanding their work and deciding what to do with it became a problem of its own. A conversation could produce a great deal, while leaving the person without a clear view of the context, the changes or the choices ahead.

Hanji grew through countless iterations around that need. Try an interaction in real work, notice what is still unclear, and refine the interface. The project became a research lab for exploring how people can interact with their new virtual companions and colleagues.

## Clarity supports judgment

When people cannot understand what an agent is doing or contributing, it is difficult to make sound judgments. Hanji's mission is to bring clarity to that interaction. Its role is a thin layer between human and agent: helping people see, question, review and direct the work.

That gives the products their purpose. Context should be understandable. Contributions should be visible. Decisions should remain open to human judgment. The interface should help people make use of the workflow as it evolves.

## Working experiments

Think, Plan and Document are today's working experiments. They explore visual thinking, coordination and knowledge, in a shared workspace with an agent conversation across the surfaces.

They are one step in the research, rather than a fixed definition of its scope. [[What Hanji is]] explains the current product; [[From idea to action]] shows how its surfaces fit together. The app is currently an invited desktop preview.

## An open, continuing practice

We now share the results publicly and as open source. The work continues as AI tools, methods and the ways people use them evolve. We want others to be able to examine, try and build on the results, and help us understand what should change next.

## Why “Hanji”

한지 is Korean paper. The name gives us a way to think about software as a thin surface that can take different forms to suit an interaction: a document, a conversation, a canvas. [[The name]] explains the metaphor.

Read [[Mission and vision]], [[Principles]] and [[The brand]] for the direction behind the work, and [[Where we are]] for its current state.

---

<!-- handbook/story/is-hanji-for-you.md -->

---
title: Is Hanji for you?
order: 40
description: Who the current preview suits, and which needs it does not yet cover.
---

# Is Hanji for you?

Hanji fits people who want a calm place to explore ideas, plan work and keep
knowledge, while retaining their own files and choosing when an agent joins in.
It can be a personal workspace or a shared instance you operate.

## The preview may fit if

- You want a canvas, planning tools and Markdown knowledge in the same workspace.
- Local folders and Git-backed content matter to you.
- You want to bring your own agent and control its access to the work.
- You are willing to use an evolving Mac preview and share feedback.
- Your team can operate its own instance or tailnet when sharing it.

## Check these limits first

The desktop is shared by invitation; there is no unrestricted public binary
download. Hosted workspace sync is not included. The app does not supply a model
account, an enterprise identity-provider integration or a procurement-ready
managed service. A teammate’s access still needs to be configured by the owner.

Local ownership also brings backup responsibilities. Repositories preserve file
history, but accounts, grants, sessions and live journals have durable state
outside those files. [[Desktop workspace]], [[Mounts]] and [[Permissions]] explain
what you are taking on.

If you need a supported hosted service or a finished enterprise deployment today,
the current preview will not cover that need. If you want to help shape a workspace
for people and agents, [request preview access](https://hanji.ink/start/).

<!-- handbook/story/mission-and-vision.md -->

---
title: Mission and vision
order: 50
description: A research lab for clearer interactions between people and agents.
---

# Mission and vision

Hanji is a research lab exploring how people interact with agents. Our mission is to bring clarity to those interactions, so people can understand what is happening, exercise sound judgment and guide what comes next.

## A thin layer between people and agents

Agents are becoming our virtual companions and colleagues. Their capabilities are changing quickly, and the ways we interact with them are still taking shape. More output or greater autonomy does not by itself make an interaction understandable. People need enough clarity to question a contribution, recognize uncertainty and make a decision.

Hanji explores that interface. It exists as a thin layer between people and agents: a surface that makes context, contributions, choices and changes easier to understand. The purpose is to help people make good use of this new workflow while keeping their judgment present.

## Born from an individual need

Hanji began with a personal need to work better with agents. It grew through countless iterations in everyday use: trying an interaction, seeing where understanding broke down, and changing the surface to make the next interaction clearer.

That remains the method. Build something useful, work with it, notice what is confusing, and iterate. The research happens through the tools and the practice of using them.

## The research, in working products

Today's workspace is one expression of that research. **Think** explores visual thinking and discussion with agents. **Plan** explores coordinating work with them. **Document** explores reading, reviewing and improving the knowledge they help produce.

The conductor brings an agent into the context of a canvas, issue or page. History, authorship, reviewable changes and supported Undo actions help make the interaction visible and open to human direction. These are current approaches to the question, and they will keep evolving.

The workspace is a working desktop preview. [[What Hanji is]] explains today's capabilities and boundaries; [[From idea to action]] shows a practical example. The larger mission is not limited to these three surfaces or to one version of the app.

## Share the results, keep learning

Hanji now shares the results publicly and as open source while continuing to iterate. Sharing makes the work available to examine, use and build on. It also opens the research to experiences beyond the individual need that started it.

AI tools, methods and working habits will keep changing. Hanji should change with them. The ambition is an ongoing practice of finding better ways to interact with our new virtual companions and colleagues.

Open formats, portable content and clear access boundaries support that practice. They are important design choices within the current products; the central question remains the quality and clarity of human–agent interaction. [[Principles]] explains the choices, and [[Where we are]] distinguishes current availability from future exploration.

---

<!-- handbook/story/principles.md -->

---
title: Principles
order: 60
---

# Principles

A short list of the beliefs Hanji is built on. When a decision is hard, these break the tie.

- **Clarity supports judgment.** Make context, contributions and choices understandable so people can question an agent's work and decide what happens next.
- **Keep the interface thin.** Give each interaction the surface it needs. The tool should help people understand and direct the work.
- **Learn through use.** Build working experiments, try them in real work and keep iterating as tools and methods change.
- **Share the results.** Publish the research and its open-source results so others can examine, use and build on the work.
- **Git holds portable content.** Document keeps Markdown in the repository and its index is rebuildable. Accounts, grants and Document comments live in durable configuration. The separate [[Think canvas]] journals accepted live edits before automatic Git checkpoints; its journal is durable too. A clone carries the checkpoint, not uncheckpointed edits.
- **The human never meets git.** Reading and writing should feel like a good editorial tool. Commits, branches, and conflicts are plumbing, and plumbing stays behind the wall until someone goes looking for it.
- **Agents are first-class readers.** Hanji treats an agent as a reader with an identity and a scope, the same as a person, and lets it propose rather than overwrite.
- **No bundled intelligence.** We do not sell you a model or meter your tokens. Bring the agent you already trust. Your bill does not grow because your team wrote more this month.
- **Permissions are honest about their limits.** We say plainly what a lock protects and what it leaves open. A promise we cannot keep is worse than no promise.
- **Byte-fidelity.** A one-word edit produces a one-line change. Your history stays readable because the tool refuses to rewrite what you did not touch.

None of these is novel on its own. Holding all of them at once, and refusing to trade one away for a feature, is the point.

# The name

한지, hanji, is traditional Korean handmade paper. The name gives the research lab a material to think with: a thin surface that takes different forms according to what people need to do.

A document, a conversation, a project canvas. Different surfaces for the same question: how can people and agents work well together?

## A surface for the interaction

Hanji's role is the layer between a person and an agent. The interface helps make context, contributions and choices understandable, leaving room for a person to question the work and decide what happens next.

The paper metaphor carries that idea into the product. The surface should be calm enough to read and think on, flexible enough to suit the interaction, and quiet enough to keep attention on the work.

## Many forms, one research direction

Think, Plan and Document are current expressions of that approach. They can change as we learn. The name belongs to the wider research into human–agent interaction, beyond any single app or arrangement of features.

Care, craft and portable content matter to the products too. [[The visual language]] describes the material choices; [[Mission and vision]] explains the research behind them.

<!-- handbook/story/why-hanji-is-different.md -->

---
title: Why Hanji is different
order: 30
description: The choices behind Hanji’s files, agent access and human surfaces.
---

# Why Hanji is different

Hanji approaches the workspace as research into human–agent interaction. The aim is to make context, contributions and decisions understandable enough for people to exercise judgment. The choices below support that work in today's products.


Hanji began with a practical need: people should be able to read and improve
knowledge that coding agents already use, without losing the files or the access
boundary. That idea now spans a canvas, a planning surface and a document reader.

## Keep the work portable

Document’s content is Markdown in repositories you control. A small page edit
should leave a small, readable diff. Plan keeps issues and projects in files.
Think uses a live journal and automatic Markdown/Git checkpoints so a canvas can
respond smoothly while accepted changes remain durable.

Portability does not mean every piece of state is in Git. Accounts, grants,
comments, sessions and uncheckpointed canvas changes need their durable stores
backed up too. The search index is a rebuildable cache; those stores are not.

## Give people the right surface

Ideas do not always start as a finished page or a fully specified task. Think
leaves space to arrange and connect them. Plan gives a next step structure.
Document keeps the context worth returning to. Shared appearance and navigation
keep those changes of surface familiar.

## Treat agents as scoped participants

The conductor is a standing conversation across the three products. It brings
context into a request and acts through the rights and scopes it has. Some
changes can be applied directly, some ask for approval, and some arrive as a
proposal for a person to review. Visible activity and supported Undo help make
those actions understandable. [[The conductor]] explains the precise behavior.

Hanji supplies no model account and meters no product feature by tokens. Provider
subscriptions and authentication remain with the tools you connect.

## Say what the boundary protects

Search, links, agent reads and publication must respect the configured access
model. The product’s checks do not hide files from someone who already has direct
repository access. [[Permissions]] documents the current checks and limits.

These are Hanji’s design choices, not a claim that no other tool shares them.
The current desktop is still an invited preview. [[Is Hanji for you?]] describes
that fit, and [[Where we are]] separates what exists from future direction.
